candidates.title: Equifinal pathways and subtypes: a developmental neuroimaging perspective on social differences in autism
candidates.abstract: Social differences are a defining feature of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). Autistic individuals show differences across multiple domains of social processing, including reciprocal behavior, social communication, and interpretation of facial expressions (Bhat et al., 2022;Lord et al., 2000). While social behavior in autistic individuals differs from that of non-autistic peers, some of these differences may also be context-dependent and reflect adaptive strategies given underlying sensory and cognitive profiles (Grace et al., 2022). Various studies have probed the neural mechanisms underlying these differences. Self-and caregiver-report studies suggest differences in social motivation in autistic individuals (Marrus et al., 2024;Neuhaus et al., 2024), and neuroimaging evidence implicates reward-related regions such as the ACC, vmPFC, OFC, amygdala, insula, and striatum (Clements et al., 2018). An alternative view emphasizes differences in understanding others' perspectives, associated with the mentalizing/Theory of Mind processes (Kanske, 2018), including medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), temporoparietal junction, and dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (Abu Hoof et al., 2025;Jayashankar et al., 2023). Additionally, co-existing hyper-and hypoconnectivity in social brain regions (Yi et al., 2022) point to the roles of developmental timing and the specificity of certain brain regions in influencing connectivity patterns in ASD (Uddin et al., 2013). This lack of generalizability reveals the biological and behavioral complexity of ASD (King et al., 2019). To reconcile these co-existing hypotheses, our opinion article introduces a two-dimensional framework-comprising functional operations and developmental spatiotemporal specificity-by selectively synthesizing evidence primarily from MRI studies published over the past decade. We suggest that these mixed empirical findings may stem from the intrinsic heterogeneity of ASD, which gives rise to multiple potential developmental pathways. Consequently, ostensibly similar social differences in ASD may represent a common behavioral outcome arising from distinct developmental alterations that progressively shape specialized brain networks.Within our two-dimensional framework (Fig. 1), the first dimension focuses on functional operations, investigating whether autistic individuals exhibit atypical neural responses for distinct components of social processing and other basic processes that shape social behavior. The social motivation hypothesis posits that autistic individuals show atypical patterns during social reward processing. A meta-analysis by Clements et al. (2018), based primarily on autistic males from childhood to adulthood without intellectual disability, reported reduced striatal responses to social and non-social rewards. However, a systematic review across multiple measures found the evidence for this hypothesis to be mixed, as reward-related differences vary by reward type, task, and brain region (Bottini, 2018). Alternatively, the mentalizing differences hypothesis proposes that social differences primarily stem from alterations in mentalizing abilities, supported by task-based evidence including only male adults (Chen et al., 2023). However, a large cross-sectional sample spanning childhood to adulthood reveals that IQ-matched autistic males and females exhibit distinct mentalizing-network restingstate connectivity, with temporoparietal hyperconnectivity in males but medial prefrontal and precuneus hypoconnectivity in females (Yang & Lee, 2018). Beyond these specifically social processes, a review integrating behavioral, electrophysiological, and neuroimaging evidence argues that atypicalities in other cognitive functions, such as motor planning and predictive control can also contribute to social differences in ASD (Casartelli et al., 2016). These foundational alterations may lead to differences in action understanding and social initiation (Casartelli et al., 2016;Kilroy et al., 2022;Stillesjö et al., 2025). Together, these findings show how atypicalities in partially distinct functional operations-reward, mentalizing, motor prediction as illustrative examples-can each manifest as social differences.The second dimension maps neurodevelopmental trajectories, examining how social phenotypes in ASD link to specific developmental windows and brain regions. Prenatally, certain types of ASD risk genes were found converging in deep-layer projection neurons of the prefrontal and motor cortices across both sexes via post-mortem analysis (Willsey et al., 2013), suggesting early vulnerability of local regions, though this does not rule out alterations in other brain regions. Structural studies of high-familial-risk infant cohorts show that, during the first year, infants who later receive an ASD diagnosis exhibit hyperexpansion of cortical surface area (Hazlett et al., 2017). These systemic alterations in perceptual, attentional, motor, and social domains often emerge before overt ASD behavioral traits manifest (Elsabbagh & Johnson, 2016). In the second year and beyond, overall brain volume overgrowth was detected, correlating with the severity of later social differences (Hazlett et al., 2017;Piven et al., 2017). Together, current findings suggest that neurodevelopmental alterations unfold across multiple developmental stages. This developmental perspective also provides a time window for interpreting the functional alterations described in the first dimension. For autistic children, resting-state evidence shows attenuated effective connectivity between the mPFC and amygdala, which are nodes shared by the mentalizing and reward networks (Li et al., 2021). By early adolescence, task-based interactive social reward elicited comparable striatal and temporoparietal responses across autistic and neurotypical groups (McNaughton et al., 2023), so neither reward-nor mentalizing-related regions showed differences in this paradigm. In autistic adults, social differences may also involve multimodal structural and functional atypicalities within the fusiform gyrus, mPFC, and amygdala (Sato & Uono, 2019). These regions are components of the 'social brain', which support processes including reward anticipation and mentalizing (Frith, 2007). Beyond these specialized circuits, multimodal evidence links autistic social differences to alterations across widespread networks (Müller & Fishman, 2018) and reduced global efficiency in the white matter connectome (Cai et al., 2022). Across these developmental stages, we propose one possible pattern-both global and localized brain alterations may coexist in early life, with atypicalities gradually emerging in higher-level functional networks as social function develops with age. However, the dominant imaging modality differs across age, so developmental shifts remain partly confounded with method. Cross-study comparisons are further limited by methodological variability-task design, head motion, medication, and scanner effects-and by the largely cross-sectional design, with longitudinal data in infancy coming from high-familial-risk cohorts whose findings may not extend to the broader autistic population. Participant samples also rarely include individuals with intellectual disability, and sex shapes mentalizing-network alterations (Yang & Lee, 2018). Such variations, however, are unlikely to fully explain the inconsistencies. The remainder points to genuine within-diagnosis heterogeneity.From heterogeneity to equifinality: rethinking social differences in ASD Our framework illustrates how heterogeneity-the biological diversity within ASD-leads to equifinality, where different developmental pathways converge onto a similar, clinically defined social phenotype. One possible explanation for the inconsistencies is the etiological heterogeneity within autistic populations (Müller & Fishman, 2018;Parellada et al., 2014). For instance, Rødgaard et al. (2019) observed a longitudinal decrease in differences between autistic and neurotypical participants from 1966 to 2019. This narrowing partly indicates broadening diagnostic criteria and highlights heterogeneity within ASD. Our framework aligns with the evidence that diverse etiological mechanisms can lead to generalized ASD traits (Fenning et al., 2019;Qi et al., 2020). This equifinality explains why heterogeneity is a barrier to understanding social differences in ASD, as a single clinical diagnosis often masks highly diverse biological pathways. Several hypotheses investigate why ASD shows this equifinality in social differences. Johnson (2017) proposed that some autistic behaviors may reflect early-life adaptation to atypical neural signal processing. For example, social withdrawal may serve as an adaptive strategy to limit sensory and cognitive input when the brain shows atypicalities in handling multidimensional, parallel, and dynamic social stimuli. On this account, the social brain network's high metabolic demand and reliance on long-range integration may render it particularly vulnerable to subtle synaptic alterations. Because such adaptation depends on compensation, environment, and learning, similar early alterations need not lead to the same outcome; the framework thus describes probabilistic rather than fixed developmental routes. Additionally, the cascade hypothesis suggests that the foundational alterations may result in missed critical social learning opportunities. For example, infants' reduced object manipulation may limit the caregiver's language input, while atypical sensory attention can affect social cue recognition. Consequently, these initial disruptions may lead to social differences (Bradshaw et al., 2022;Iverson et al., 2023). If diverse pathways converge on similar social outcomes, the research task becomes to delineate these distinct pathways-that is, to identify meaningful biological subtypes. Our framework makes a further prediction: autistic individuals matched on similar socialcommunication profiles are predicted to show distinguishable longitudinal network trajectories. Classifying more homogeneous subgroups within ASD may address this heterogeneity (Harris, 2019;Rødgaard et al., 2019). For example, Litman et al. (2025) identified four geneticdevelopmental subtypes. These subtypes-moderate challenges, broadly affected, social or behavioral, and mixed ASD with developmental delay-correlated with specific sets of genetic alterations acting at variable developmental windows (prenatal to adolescence). In terms of brain networks, Lombardo et al. (2019) identified a subtype that features early visual-social engagement differences, associated with hypoconnectivity between the default mode network and occipitotemporal cortex. At the micro-level, subtype-specific gene sets are linked to different molecular signaling pathways, involving immune and synapse function, G-protein-coupled receptor signaling, and protein synthesis (Buch et al., 2023). Taken together, while these criteria of classification vary, they may not be mutually exclusive. In fact, this evidence depicts several potential links on how developmental timing, as well as genetic or neural pathways shape ASD phenotypes.Our framework locates social differences in ASD within interacting networks that develop over time, rather than in fixed core regions. We propose that social differences should be viewed as the convergent outcome of various alterations across a wide range of neural networks. Importantly, the so-called social brain is increasingly viewed as an interconnected 'social connectome' including cooperating and overlapping networks (Maliske et al., 2023;Maliske & Kanske, 2022;Schurz et al., 2020). Because social cognition draws on brain regions involved in perception, motor skills, and attention (Van Overwalle, 2009), alterations in these foundational levels can cascade upward to social differences (Iverson et al., 2023). Unlike models that describe how these alterations arise or spread, our framework maps where to look for them-at which developmental stage and in which operation. Future work should consider developmental timing to explore whether these atypical developments are due to prenatal or genetic factors, or to the cascading effects of synaptic pruning. In addition, rather than focusing solely on one mechanism that fits the broad ASD criteria defined by behavioral traits, future studies should emphasize identifying subtypes characterized by divergent neural developmental trajectories. Indeed, recent advances have identified distinct ASD subtypes based on brain connectivity patterns and developmental timing (Litman et al., 2025;Liu et al., 2025;Qiao et al., 2025). However, valid ASD subtypes should reflect coherent neurodevelopmental pathways rather than mere statistical clusters, which are sensitive to analytical choices. More fundamentally, whether heterogeneity is discrete or continuous remains an open question for future research. Ideally, these pathways should exhibit longitudinal stability and neurobiological coherence across developmental trajectories and show external clinical validity, including the ability to predict behavioral profiles and intervention response. Understanding the neurodevelopmental evolution of these subtypes could then enhance the interpretability and replicability of studies and guide precise interventions (Kamp-Becker et al., 2017;Liu et al., 2025). Such subtyping efforts may facilitate more tailored interventions for specific autistic subgroups. For instance, preliminary evidence suggests that some autistic individuals with reward-network alterations may benefit from interventions targeting social reward processing (Baker et al., 2020), although whether reward-network-defined subtypes predict treatment response remains to be established. Developmental timing is also critical, as evidence supports the importance of early intervention during periods of heightened neuroplasticity (Bradshaw et al., 2022;Iverson et al., 2023;Nelson et al., 2024), despite limited evidence for imaging-defined subtype-specific early interventions. Finally, because social differences can emerge as an adaptive response to reduce cognitive load (Johnson, 2017), interventions should be carefully evaluated for potential anxiety, distress, or other unintended effects, given concerns about incomplete adverse-event reporting (Bottema-Beutel et al., 2021). Therefore, interventions should support sensory and cognitive mechanisms while also considering an autistic individual's support level. For now, our framework guides future stratification research rather than clinical decision-making. To sum up, we argue that embracing equifinality and mapping functional operations onto developmental spatiotemporal trajectories can enable biologically grounded subtyping and, ultimately, more humane, individualized support that prioritizes autonomy and quality of life over the normalization of social behavior. mentalizing/theory of mind (blue), and motor prediction and other cognitive functions (coral); green marks regions where the social motivation and mentalizing/theory of mind operations overlap. Solid outlines denote supported findings; the dashed cell denotes a non-confirmatory finding (no group difference). Prenatal-infancy alterations are not functionally specific and are therefore placed below the functional axis rather than assigned to a single operation. Abbreviations: fMRI, functional magnetic resonance imaging; mPFC, medial prefrontal cortex; MRI, magnetic resonance imaging; rs-fMRI, resting-state functional MRI.

candidates.title: How large language models judge and influence human cooperation
candidates.abstract: Humans increasingly rely on large language models (LLMs) to support decisions in social settings. Previous work suggests that such tools can shape people's moral judgments. However, how LLMs evaluate decisions in social dilemmas, and the long-term implications of LLM-based assessments on human cooperation-driven by indirect reciprocity, reputations, and the capacity to judge interactions of others-remain unclear. We evaluate the social norms of 21 state-of-the-art LLMs when judging more than 40,000 fictitious decisions in social dilemmas. Through an evolutionary game-theoretical model, we study prosociality in populations adhering to these norms, theoretically studying their potential impact on long-term human cooperation. We observe a remarkable agreement in LLMs when evaluating actions against opponents perceived as good. Yet, there is large within- and between-model variance when assessing actions toward ill-reputed individuals. Our theoretical analysis reveals that these differences can significantly impact the prevalence of cooperation within our model. Finally, we show that prompt-based interventions can steer LLM norms, particularly when these define objective goals. Our theoretical model links LLM-based advice to long-term social dynamics, highlighting the importance of designing LLM norms considering their potential effects on human cooperation.

candidates.title: Empathic Concern for Violators Modulates Victims' Evaluation of Third-Party Punishment Outcomes: Behavioral and EEG Evidence
candidates.abstract: When fairness conflicts with empathy-induced altruism, victims often reduce punishment to protect violators' welfare. Whether this influence extends to outcome evaluations when punishment is implemented by third parties remains unclear. We combined an adapted Third-Party Dictator Game with electroencephalography (EEG) to address this. Participants received unfair allocations from violators and evaluated third-party punishment (TPP) outcomes. Empathic concern was induced by portraying violators as being in need. Behaviorally, victims in the empathy (vs. non-empathy) condition rated no-punishment and partial-punishment outcomes as more appropriate but complete-punishment outcomes as less appropriate. Partial-punishment outcomes received the highest ratings in the empathy condition, reflecting a balance between protecting violators' welfare and restoring fairness. Neurally, partial-punishment outcomes induced smaller P2 amplitudes in the empathy (vs. non-empathy) condition, suggesting lower motivational salience because they better matched victims' goals. No-punishment outcomes induced larger LPP amplitudes in the empathy (vs. non-empathy) condition, reflecting sustained processing of their affective and motivational significance. Parietal alpha suppression was weaker in the empathy (vs. non-empathy) condition, indicating reduced sustained attention to TPP outcomes. Together, these findings suggest that empathic concern shapes victims' evaluations of third-party norm-enforcement outcomes, extending its influence beyond contexts in which the empathizing individual also implements punishment.

candidates.title: From Self to Others? Testing Whether Brief Mindfulness Reduces Intergroup Bias through Decentering or Self-Compassion
candidates.abstract: AbstractBrief mindfulness reliably changes how individuals relate to their own internal experiences, but whether these intrapersonal changes generalize to intergroup responding remains unclear. This preregistered experiment (N = 91) examined whether mindfulness-related processes—decentering and compassionate self-responding—were associated with socio-affective responses toward in-group and out-group members. Participants completed an adapted Socio-affective Video Task using AI-generated images to assess compassion, personal distress, and prosocial giving. Brief mindfulness was significantly linked to increased decentering and compassionate self-responding. Contrary to preregistered hypotheses, the intervention did not reduce intergroup bias in compassion, personal distress, or the empathic Dictator Game. Findings suggest that brief mindfulness primarily influences proximal intrapersonal processes, whereas changes in intergroup socio-affective responding may be limited.

candidates.title: Behavior is Not Enough: A Mechanism-Based Evaluation of Social Norm Emergence in LLM Societies
candidates.abstract: Social norms cannot be identified from behavior alone: the same cooperative equilibrium may reflect shared expectations, strategic incentives, or simple imitation. Yet in multi-agent large language model systems, prior work largely treats behavioral convergence as evidence of norm emergence. In this work, we introduce an evaluation framework that measures agents' reported empirical and normative expectations in addition to behavioral convergence. Through controlled ablations, we test the effect of expectation elicitation and isolate two collective mechanisms central to theories of norm formation---social learning through interaction and social selection through network-based group formation. We further test the stability of these resulting dynamics under adversarial disruption across four LLM families. We find that eliciting expectations increases cooperative contributions, while social learning stabilizes behavior, and social selection reliably identifies cooperators but provides limited behavioral reinforcement. Following disruption, normative expectations and behavioral coordination recover differently. Together, these results show that similar cooperative outcomes can arise from different underlying social processes. By making expectations observable, our framework allows us to attribute each mechanism's contribution separately, offering designers of multi-agent systems a principled basis for selecting the social processes that sustain cooperation.

candidates.title: Learning to cooperate in a changing world: How caring about the future promotes cooperation across scales
candidates.abstract: In social dilemmas, individuals need to forgo short-term temptations to achieve synergistic collective outcomes through cooperation. Previous work has examined mechanisms through which cooperation can evolve, including direct reciprocity, indirect reciprocity, environmental stochasticity, network reciprocity, and demographic stochasticity. These mechanisms have largely been studied under natural selection or social learning. As the other side of the same coin, it is equally important to study cooperation under self-learning, where individuals adapt based on their own experiences. Here, we focus on the dynamics of multi-agent reinforcement learning and derive analytical conditions under which these mechanisms can stabilize cooperation under learning dynamics across scales. We find that reinforcement learning can steer self-interested individuals toward cooperation when agents value the future over short-term temptation. Our work provides a unified approach to identifying the determinants of learning to cooperate in a changing world, thereby paving the way for the advancement of cooperative artificial intelligence.

candidates.title: Convergence and Divergence: Forces Shaping Marmoset Vocal and Social Interactions
candidates.venue: Zurich Open Repository and Archive (University of Zurich)
candidates.abstract: Human language hinges on a remarkable capacity for vocal production learning, yet the evolutionary origins of this ability remain poorly understood. This thesis explores the idea that increasing cooperation and social interdependence played a major role in the evolution of vocal flexibility in the hominin lineage. To investigate this possibility, I studied common marmosets (Callithrix jacchus), a primate that shares several socio-communicative traits with humans, including cooperative breeding, proactive prosociality, vocal turn-taking, infant babbling and vocal convergence. The thesis begins by examining how learning emerges through social interactions. A review of the literature highlights the importance of contingent social feedback in shaping development, learning, and coordination. In cooperative breeding systems, interactions with multiple caregivers create rich opportunities for social learning and may provide conditions that favor the evolution of flexible communication. The first empirical study investigated vocal accommodation during pair formation as a process of vocal convergence. Newly paired marmosets gradually modified their vocalizations to become more similar to one another. Mathematical modeling suggested that this process is driven by continuous auditory-guided adjustments based on partner vocalizations. These findings indicate that vocal flexibility in marmosets is an active, socially mediated process, providing insight into mechanisms that may represent evolutionary precursors of more advanced vocal production learning. The second empirical study examined vigilance coordination during feeding. Marmosets coordinated these behaviors through anti-phase synchronization and convergence of rhythms. This coordination resulted in longer uninterrupted feeding bouts and emerged through continuous adjustments to partner behavior. Similar interactional dynamics were observed in both vocal accommodation and vigilance coordination, suggesting that communication and cooperation rely on common mechanisms of social synchrony. The third empirical study examined the role of vocal divergence in social boundary formation. While individuals vocally converged within groups, neighboring groups actively diverged from one another, demonstrating that the same vocal flexibility underlying convergence can also generate divergence, contributing to both within-group social cohesion and between-group boundary maintenance. The results parallel processes underlying dialect formation in humans and provide evidence that socially driven vocal differentiation is not unique to our species. The final empirical chapter examined whether vocal convergence in marmosets is socially regulated and whether individuals hold strong expectations about how social partners should vocalize during interactions. Within an interactive closed-loop playback paradigm, marmosets engaged in natural vocal exchanges with a speaker wherein playbacks were generated to either converge toward or diverge away from the focal's calls. Marmosets responded positively to converging calls and negatively to diverging calls, and they actively modified their own vocalizations to re-establish similarity following divergence from the speaker. These findings suggest that vocal convergence carries social significance and may function as a socially regulated norm. Taken together, the findings show that convergence and divergence are fundamental forces shaping marmoset vocal and social behavior. Vocal convergence, behavioral synchrony, vocal divergence, and social reinforcement come out as interconnected aspects of a communication system shaped by life in highly interdependent social groups. More generally, the results support the view that vocal production learning evolved gradually from ancestral forms of vocal plasticity already present in primates. Cooperative social systems may have provided the selective pressures under which increasingly flexible forms of vocal behavior became advantageous. Vocal accommodation offers a plausible starting point for this process because it already involves auditory monitoring, vocal modification, and social feedback. Overall, this thesis argues that cooperation and communication evolved in close association. The findings support the hypothesis that increasing social interdependence, cooperative breeding, and contingent social interactions were important factors in the evolutionary pathway leading from ancestral primate vocal flexibility to the full-fledged vocal production learning that underlies human language.

candidates.title: Artificial Intelligence in Education: Principles, Applications, Challenges, and Future Perspectives
candidates.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
candidates.abstract: We live at a hinge point in the history of education. For more than a century, schools, colleges, and training institutions have refined methods that scale instruction through curricula, standardized assessments, and classroom routines. Today, artificial intelligence is opening new pathways that promise to reshape those methods at scale while also making learning more personal, timely, and relevant. This book Artificial Intelligence in Education: Principles, Applications, Challenges, and Future Perspectives offers a comprehensive guide to that transformation. It is written for educators, policymakers, instructional designers, technologists, and researchers who want a rigorous, practical, and ethically grounded exploration of how AI can support learning across contexts and life stages. AI has moved from narrow lab demonstrations into tools used every day: adaptive quizzes that adjust to student mastery, automated essay feedback systems, chatbots that answer routine student questions, and immersive learning environments that combine AI with virtual and augmented reality. The COVID-19 pandemic accelerated many of these adoptions and exposed stark inequalities in access, teacher preparedness, and policy frameworks. Simultaneously, breakthroughs in large language models, multimodal learning, and scalable analytics have raised both excitement and concern. Educators and decision-makers urgently need a resource that synthesizes technical foundations, pedagogical design, ethical guardrails, and empirical evidence—while also charting future research directions. This book responds to that need. The book is organized into eleven parts and thirty-four chapters that move from foundations to applications, from tools for classroom practice to governance, and from present deployments to future possibilities. Each part deliberately balances technical explanation with educational significance. Chapters explain underlying AI methods in accessible language, then demonstrate how those methods map to concrete educational tasks—assessment, tutoring, curriculum design, classroom management, and institutional planning. Where possible, chapters include case studies and examples to ground theory in practice. Key Aims Clarify Fundamentals: Many educators encounter AI as buzzwords. Part I and the technical chapters (Parts II–III) unpack core concepts—machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, and computer vision—in ways that show what these tools can and cannot do in educational contexts. Bridge Research and Practice: The book aims to help researchers design studies with educational validity and help practitioners choose and implement AI tools responsibly. Case studies, implementation notes, and chapters on tools for teachers (Part IV) serve this bridge-building function. Center People and Pedagogy: Technology should serve learning goals, not the other way around. Throughout the book, emphasis returns to pedagogical principles: personalization that supports mastery rather than mere individualization; assessments that inform learning rather than only rank students; and teacher roles that shift toward facilitation and interpretation. Surface Ethics, Policy, and Governance: Part VII foregrounds fairness, privacy, transparency, and accountability. AI systems can amplify biases, create privacy risks, and obscure decision pathways. We map legal and normative frameworks—international guidelines, national policies, and institutional governance—to practical recommendations for safer deployments. Encourage Critical, Forward-Looking Research: The concluding parts outline emerging research agendas—explainable AI, emotional and multimodal learning systems, AI literacy, and equity-focused studies—and propose methodological approaches for rigorous evaluation. Educators and instructional designers will find practical frameworks for selecting and integrating AI tools into curricula, formative assessment, and classroom practice. School and university leaders will find guidance on governance, procurement, privacy, and institutional analytics. Policymakers will gain an overview of regulatory and ethical challenges and proposed policymaking pathways that protect learners while enabling beneficial innovation. Researchers will find a consolidated reference that ties technical methods to educational constructs, highlights gaps in evidence, and suggests promising directions for inquiry. Developers and edtech entrepreneurs will gain insight into educational needs, evaluation criteria, and ethical design priorities that increase the likelihood of real-world impact. Highlights of the Book Foundations: The first three chapters set the stage by tracing the evolution of AI and educational technology, clarifying definitions, and situating AIED historically and conceptually. Technologies: Parts II and III explain machine learning, deep learning, NLP, and computer vision, with clear mappings to educational use cases such as student modeling, automated feedback, and classroom monitoring. Practice: Parts IV–VI focus on the teacher and learner experience—intelligent tutoring systems, personalized learning pathways, assessment innovations, and AI-driven curriculum tools. Emerging Tech: Robotics, AR/VR, and IoT are treated not as curiosities but as components of comprehensive learning ecosystems. Analytics and Research: The book addresses methodological issues in learning analytics and educational data mining, offering researchers templates for analysis and evaluation. Governance and Equity: Dedicated sections examine ethics, privacy, policy frameworks, and practical steps institutions can take to ensure responsible adoption. Case Studies and Research Agenda: The final parts synthesize international case studies, extract best practices, and propose an agenda for future scholarship and innovation. AI carries enormous potential for improving access, tailoring instruction, and providing actionable insights at scale. Yet it also presents real hazards: reproducing societal biases, eroding privacy, over-promising efficacy, and diverting scarce resources toward flashy but low-impact solutions. This book advocates a pragmatic middle path: pursue innovation while committing to evidence-based evaluation, participatory design that includes teachers and learners, transparent reporting of benefits and harms, and policies that prioritize equity. How to Use This Book Read Linearly for a Full Course: The book is structured so an instructor, researcher, or administrator new to AIED can progress from basics to advanced topics. Consult Copically: Practitioners can jump to chapters on assessment, tutoring systems, or classroom management as needed. Use as a Course Text: Instructors can assign chapters for modules in educational technology, instructional design, or AIED-focused seminars. Use for Research Planning: Researchers will find the methodological and future-research chapters useful when designing studies, and the case studies useful for comparative analysis. The field of AIED is dynamic. New algorithms, models, and deployments appear rapidly; empirical evidence varies in quality and generalizability; and social contexts differ across regions. Where empirical findings exist, chapters summarize and critique the evidence. Where evidence is thin, authors point to open questions and suggest study designs. Readers should treat this book as both a synthesis of current knowledge and a living prompt for continued examination and experimentation.As you read, I invite you to engage critically: test assumptions, pilot ideas with small cohorts, measure outcomes against learning goals, and foreground learner dignity and agency. Use the book as a toolkit for designing learning environments where AI amplifies human strengths—curiosity, creativity, empathy, and critical thinking—rather than replaces them.If you are a researcher, let this book suggest experiments, measurement approaches, and ethical frameworks that will sharpen the evidence base. If you are a teacher, let it suggest practical ways to reduce cognitive load, increase timely feedback, and personalize pathways while preserving social learning. If you are a policymaker, let it frame policy choices that protect learners and enable beneficial innovation. We stand at the start of new educational possibilities. May this book inform your decisions, inspire your research, and help shape AI in education that is effective, equitable, and humane.

candidates.title: Land subdivision and pro-social preferences: Evidence from Maasai land
candidates.abstract: We study whether the subdivision of communal grazing grounds affect how Maasai play with co-villagers in a series of games: a reverse dictator game, a public goods game, a trust game, and an insurance game. We collect data in 4 locations, in Kenya and Tanzania. In Kenya we have access to respondents from subdivided and non-subdivided group ranches. The subdivided group ranch is located in a wet area, and the non-subdivided ranch is located in a dry area. candidates.title: The Bloodied Dog and the Guilty Master: How Suspicion Turns Misconception into a Verdict — and Prejudice into Violence
candidates.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
candidates.abstract: This essay examines how the human behaviour of suspicion turns incomplete evidence into presumed guilt and prejudice into harm. It begins with Odysseus’s companions opening the bag of winds because they suspect that he has concealed treasure from them. It then centres upon Ibn al-Marzubān’s account in his The Merits of Dogs over Those Who Wear Clothes, of a man who sees blood on his dog’s muzzle, assumes that it has killed his child and kills the animal before discovering that it had in fact protected the child from a viper. Read alongside al-Ghazzālī’s teachings on bad opinion, rancour, backbiting and companionship, the story shows how suspicion corrupts judgement, breaks trust and enables slander. The essay traces the same failure through racism, misinformation, public accusation and political manipulation. It argues for verification, restraint, dignified correction and the prevention of greater harm. Across Ithaca, Baghdad and the modern world, the faithful dog exposes how easily human beings abandon loyalty, reciprocity and fairness.

candidates.title: Developing a Mealtime Assistance Framework for Geriatric Psychiatric Inpatients: A Narrative Review
candidates.abstract: IntroductionMalnutrition is highly prevalent amongst psychiatric inpatients, with prevalence reaching up to 42.5%. Geriatric-psychiatric inpatients, in particular, face complex nutritional barriers distinct from typical hospital malnutrition. To date, there is limited guidance on adapting mealtime assistance strategies to the complex needs of geriatric-psychiatric inpatients.MethodsA systematized narrative review aligned with SANRA was conducted to develop a mealtime assistance framework. Personal and institutional challenges in geriatric-psychiatric care were identified, followed by a review of successful mealtime practices from various inpatient settings, and then key elements were modified to fit the unique needs of the target population.ResultsPersonal challenges to addressing malnutrition in geriatric psychiatric care include medication-induced appetite and taste changes, apathy, low motivation, and altered circadian rhythm patterns. Institutional barriers include overly rigid organizational approaches, deficits in staff knowledge relating to evidence-based nutrition, competing staff priorities and a predominant focus on pharmacotherapy, which may cause approaches to physical health and nutritional status to be inadequate. Key nutritional interventions from the literature include improving the mealtime environment through protected mealtimes and auditory optimization, enhancing human interaction between staff and patients, implementing a 'train-the-trainer' model, and using oral nutritional supplements and food fortification. Key adaptations to address specific challenges in this population include flexible mealtime scheduling to accommodate disrupted routines, specialized staff training in patient empathy and mutual reciprocity, and the use of sealed packaging for oral nutrition supplements to address paranoia.ConclusionImplementing mealtime interventions tailored explicitly to the geriatric psychiatric inpatient population is vital for addressing malnutrition and improving both physical and mental health outcomes. This review provides a novel, setting-specific mealtime assistance framework for this uniquely vulnerable population, making testing and cost-effectiveness analysis an important priority for future research.

candidates.title: The Structure of Social Cognition: Precursors, Mechanisms, and Competencies
candidates.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
candidates.abstract: Social competence is an architecture rather than a unitary capacity, and the cognitive science of social behaviour remains fragmentedacross disciplines that do not always share a vocabulary. We propose a three-level decomposition, drawing on cognitive science,developmental psychology, philosophy of mind, psycholinguistics, social ethology and AI research. Seven candidate socio-cognitiveprecursors (embodied, pre-representational dispositions such as animacy detection, gaze following and emotional contagion) sitbelow seven socio-cognitive mechanisms (goal inference, mentalizing, mutual modelling, shared intentionality, meta-cognitive socialmodelling, norm representation, reciprocity tracking), which compose into thirty-eight domain competencies. The mechanisms areindividuated by dissociability and ordered by their dependencies, with the evidence stated for each boundary. That ordering carriesour main structural claim: goal inference, not mentalizing, is the foundational mechanism, and coordination, joint commitment andcommon ground (short of its epistemic form) do not require belief attribution. This departs from the theory-of-mind-centred accountsthe field has organised itself around. We also discuss two factors that are not specific to social cognition, yet play a fundamental role init: situatedness, and central coherence, which we argue is a parameter on belief inference rather than a socio-cognitive mechanismper-se. Finally, we compile a catalogue of experimental paradigms, including matched “fine-cuts” task pairs that separate surface socialperformance from socio-cognitive competence, and set out how the framework could be tested by socio-cognitive ablation.

candidates.title: Indigenous Marriage Counselling as a Psychosocial System: Cultural Practices, Psychological Mechanisms and Marital Regulation in South Sudan
candidates.abstract: Marriage in South Sudan operates simultaneously as an intimate partnership, a kinship arrangement and a community institution. This article examines indigenous marriage counselling as a psychosocial system rather than as a collection of isolated customs. Drawing primarily on the first two objectives of a doctoral study—identifying traditional marriage counselling practices and the psychological principles embedded within them—the paper analyses how elders’ guidance, family participation, cultural instruction, mediation and reconciliation function as mechanisms of behavioural learning, emotional regulation, social accountability and relational repair. The underlying study employed a mixed-methods descriptive cross-sectional design. Of 250 questionnaires distributed, 242 were returned (96.8%). The six-item traditional counselling scale produced a mean of 4.30 (SD=0.79; Cronbach’s α=.849). Traditional leaders’ role in resolving marital conflicts received the strongest endorsement (M=4.48), while all six items recorded at least 84% agreement or strong agreement. Open-ended responses identified respect, communication, trust, cooperation, elders, family support and cultural or religious values as recurrent resources for successful marriage. The analysis interprets these practices through Family Systems Theory, Social Learning Theory, Attachment Theory, Cognitive Behavioural Theory and Ecological Systems Theory. The findings suggest that indigenous counselling can be understood as a layered psychosocial regulatory system: it teaches marital norms, creates culturally legitimate spaces for dialogue, mobilises support networks, reinforces accountability, and facilitates reconciliation. However, these strengths do not justify uncritical preservation. Risks involving confidentiality, unequal authority, coercion, violence and complex psychological problems require safeguarding and professional referral. The article concludes that culturally responsive marriage counselling in South Sudan should preserve beneficial indigenous mechanisms while distinguishing community guidance from professional psychological treatment and high-risk safeguarding functions.

candidates.title: Modulation of vicarious fear extinction with oxytocin in social anxiety disorder
candidates.abstract: Abstract Approximately half of patients with social anxiety disorder (SAD) do not achieve remission from cognitive behavioral therapy, which relies on direct extinction of social fears. Direct extinction can be inefficient and costly; social learning theories propose that social fears may be extinguished vicariously through others’ safety experiences. Potentiating vicarious extinction through pharmacologic agents such as oxytocin, an endogenous neuromodulator involved in social affiliation and fear regulation, may offer a novel strategy for augmenting extinction in SAD. We hypothesized that vicarious extinction would reduce conditioned threat responses in SAD, oxytocin would potentiate the effects of vicarious extinction, and oxytocin’s effects would be moderated by gender. In this randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study, participants ( n = 104; n = 51 SAD, n = 53 healthy controls) first completed an acquisition procedure outside of the scanner, and received 24 IU intranasal oxytocin or matching placebo prior to completing a vicarious extinction and reinstatement test while undergoing fMRI and recording skin conductance responses (SCR). During acquisition, there was a significant main effect of stimulus type, as all participants displayed greater SCR in CS+s compared to CS-, suggesting that the task was effective in evoking conditioned threat. SCR findings partially supported a pattern of attenuated conditioned threat responses to the vicariously extinguished cue (CS + S) compared to the unextinguished cue (CS + R), but there remained a significant difference between the CS + S and CS-, and this was evident across all participants, not just in SAD. fMRI results did not reveal benefits of vicarious extinction in SAD. Contrary to hypotheses, there were no effects of diagnostic group or drug condition or their interaction; oxytocin showed no effects on SCRs or brain responses to CS + R versus CS + S cues. However, as expected, oxytocin demonstrated gender-dependent effects, as fMRI results showed significant drug by gender interactions in the amygdala, insula, hippocampus, and ventromedial prefrontal cortex, with oxytocin increasing threat responding to vicariously non-extinguished CS+ in men compared to women. Findings underscore effects of oxytocin that vary by gender in fear regulation-related neural circuitry.

candidates.title: From Preference to Reciprocity: Decentralized Matching with Empirically Grounded LLM-agent Based Modeling
candidates.abstract: Bipartite matching is a fundamental problem in game theory and market design. Classical approaches such as Gale--Shapley assume complete preferences and centralized computation, whereas many real-world matching processes are decentralized, asynchronous, and shaped by sequential interaction under limited information. We propose a dynamic bipartite matching framework that combines large language model (LLM) agents with contextual bandits. In a simulated Chinese marriage market, economically grounded LLM agents evaluate locally encountered candidates, while agent-specific Logistic-UCB models learn reciprocal acceptance from realized proposal outcomes. The mechanism therefore separates two decisions---\emph{whom do I like?} and \emph{who is likely to like me back?}---without requiring ex ante market-wide preference rankings. We first validate LLM-induced mate preferences against the empirical conditional-logit reference across multiple LLM backbones. In the $50\times50$ matching experiment, Bandit-UCB achieves the highest mean mutual welfare (56.01 versus 54.87 for Gale--Shapley), a smaller gender rank gap than the classical baselines, and the fewest blocking pairs among the LLM-ABM policies. Learned acceptance models show economically interpretable gender-differentiated associations, while counterfactual setups reveal no systematic unilateral advantage from prior search knowledge. Overall, these results support the advantages of decentralized matching with LLM-based behavioral modeling and online learning under incomplete information for economic simulation and computational social science research.

candidates.title: COOPERATION WITHOUT A PARTNER: THE MIGRATION OF PRAGMATIC LABOUR IN USER–AI DISCOURSE
candidates.abstract: This article describes the communicative situation created by the spread of conversational interfaces built on large language models, a situation for which linguistic theory was not designed: users mitigate directives, thank the system and apologise for their own imprecision, although a language model holds no beliefs, assumes no obligations and possesses no face requiring protection. Pragmatic description of this behaviour is entirely successful, yet the frameworks themselves presuppose communicative intention on both sides. The article examines what becomes of pragmatic competence once that presupposition is withdrawn. It argues that established frameworks retain their descriptive adequacy while surrendering their reciprocity: they no longer model an exchange between interlocutors but the sustained pragmatic work of a single participant, directed at an addressee that can neither endorse nor return it. The theoretical groundwork is laid by J. Austin, J. Searle, H. P. Grice, S. Levinson, D. Sperber and D. Wilson, G. Leech, P. Brown and J. Habermas; the survival of social norms in machine-directed speech is explained by B. Reeves, C. Nass and Y. Moon, A. Gambino, J. Fox and R. Ratan; empirical refinement comes from L. Panfili, R. Bowman, Z. Yin and E. Miehling; the applied dimension from J. White and J. D. Zamfirescu-Pereira, the metapragmatic from C. Caffi and J. Verschueren, the sociolinguistic from P. Joshi, A. Radford, L. Bilaniuk and S. Sokolova. The study employs critical analysis and synthesis of sources, conceptual analysis of pragmatic categories with respect to their reciprocity requirement, comparison of the status of the maxims in human dialogue and in user–AI discourse, and the modelling of a two-level account of the artificial addressee. Established frameworks are shown to retain their descriptive adequacy while surrendering their reciprocity: interpretive labour migrates to the user, and the Gricean maxims are re-encoded from expectations into design specifications within the prompt. The contradiction between automatic and strategic politeness is resolved through a distinction between an agent model and a resource model of the system, and the term operational politeness is proposed. Assistant-directed code-switching is reclassified as compensation for asymmetric channel availability, so that speakers of thinly resourced languages carry an inferential and a channel burden at once. Prospects for further study lie in eliciting a corpus of machine-directed speech from Ukrainian users, testing the distinction between inferential and channel burden against languages of comparable resourcing status, and reconceiving prompt design within AI-literacy curricula as a linguistic rather than a technical skill.

candidates.title: Contextual Interpersonal Calibration (CIC): An Iterative Method for Autistic Adults Decoding Implicit Communicative Codes in Neurotypical-Dominant Environments
candidates.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
candidates.abstract: Contextual Interpersonal Calibration (CIC) is a method for autistic adults decoding implicit communicative codes in neurotypical-majority environments, formalized here as an explicit, iterative alternative to communicative intuition. The method proceeds through a recursive cycle of observation, local hypothesis, register selection, and falsification, tracked across six operational variables including cognitive cost. CIC positions itself relative to Communication Accommodation Theory, single-case ABAB experimental design, and Bayesian models of social inference, combining elements of each into a procedure usable in real time without training in any of the three fields. The method functions as a bridge rather than a permanent adaptation: it represents only the autistic person's half of a relational approach, with reciprocity from the interlocutor tracked as a variable subject to the same falsification discipline as any other hypothesis. CIC is presented as an operational proposal grounded in nearly fifty years of the author's own recursive practice; the literature cited documents the communicative problem it responds to and the theoretical precedents the procedure draws on, rather than validating the procedure's own efficacy.
