candidates.abstract: This deposit contains analysis code and supporting materials accompanying the manuscript “Neural arbitration between social learning strategies depends on others’ reliability.” The archive includes behavioral analyses, hierarchical computational models implemented in Stan, WAIC model comparison, parameter and model recovery, whole-brain and ROI-based fMRI analyses, and scripts for reproducing individual manuscript figure panels. Behavioral data, numerical summaries, fixed ROI masks, and figure outputs are included. Reproduction instructions are provided in README.md and PUBLICATION.html, with Python dependencies pinned in uv.lock. Individual neuroimaging derivatives and large model-fitting artifacts are not included. The code is released under the MIT License.

candidates.title: Characterize the Neural Representation of Vicarious Threat and Safety Learning in Social Anxiety Disorder
candidates.abstract: This analysis plan describes a multivoxel fMRI investigation of neural representations underlying vicarious threat and safety learning during fear extinction in social anxiety disorder (SAD). The central research question is: can neural representations associated with vicarious threat and safety learning be detected during fear extinction phase in SAD, and how is it different from the neural representations of healthy controls (HC). The primary focus is on the updating process that occurs during extinction, when previously acquired threat and safety information is being revised in response to new experience by a demonstrator. Accordingly, the analyses are designed to characterize neural representations expressed while this updating process is occurring, rather than to classify participants or individual trials according to whether extinction learning is “successful” or “unsuccessful”. Learning outcome is therefore not used as a grouping factor at either the participant or trial level. Instead, trial-level neural responses to the vicariously reinforced threat cue (CSR) and vicarious safety cue (CSS) are used to identify and characterize the neural information distinguishing threat from safety during extinction. A second central objective is to determine how the neural organization of vicarious threat and safety learning differs between SAD and HC participants. SAD may involve alterations in the representation and updating of threat and safety information. The analysis therefore does not assume that a single neural signature generalizes across diagnostic groups. Instead, neural representations are first identified separately within SAD and HC participants, allowing the spatial distribution and discriminability of threat- and safety-related information to differ between groups. The resulting neural profiles are then compared directly to test whether SAD is associated with altered representational geometry, classification certainty, or temporal learning dynamics. The experimental design also includes intranasal oxytocin administered immediately before the extinction phase. Because oxytocin was hypothesized to modulate neural processes involved in threat and safety updating, its administration could alter the very neural representations that the primary analyses seek to identify. Therefore, the initial identification and characterization of threat-safety representations are performed in the placebo condition only, providing an estimate of extinction-related neural representations without potential pharmacological modulation. Participants receiving oxytocin are subsequently incorporated into dedicated analyses testing whether oxytocin alters these neural profiles and whether such effects differ between SAD and HC participants. Within this framework, the primary decoding analysis focuses on the vicariously reinforced threat cue (CSR) and the vicarious safety cue (CSS) because both underwent vicarious learning but acquired different meanings. CSR versus CSS decoding therefore directly tests whether multivoxel neural patterns during extinction distinguish vicariously learned threat from vicariously learned safety. The nonreinforced safety cue (CS−) has a different learning history and is therefore not included as a third class in the primary decoder. Instead, CS− is used as a safety reference condition in subsequent representational analyses, allowing the relative positions of CSR and CSS to be interpreted with respect to an established safety representation and enabling examination of whether CSS becomes more similar to CS− during extinction. L2-regularized logistic regression will be employed to test whether vicarious safety and threat learning are represented by group-specific neural signatures in patients with social anxiety disorder (SAD) and healthy controls (HC) respectively. Next, the neural representations of vicarious learning will be characterized by examining representational geometry, decision-certainty metrics, and single-trial learning dynamics. Then, associations will be tested between these neural profiles and skin conductance responses (SCR), clinical symptoms, and oxytocin modulation. Finally, the neural representations detected during fear extinction will be examined during the reinstatement phase to test whether neural representations of vicarious threat and safety learning are maintained in reinstatement.

candidates.title: Co-regulation of learning in simulation: A qualitative exploration of experiences, manifestations, enablers and barriers in medical student simulations
candidates.venue: Focus on Health Professional Education A Multi-Professional Journal
candidates.abstract: Background: Medical education literature offers limited insights into the presence and potential of co-regulated learning (CoRL), where learners interact reciprocally, particularly in collaborative settings such as simulation-based education (SBE). Our qualitative study explores CoRL within SBE in an undergraduate medical program, describing its manifestations, enablers and barriers. Methods: Employing a constructivist approach and reflexive thematic analysis, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 30 participants across four groups: medical students (n = 13), facilitators (n = 5), simulated patients (n = 6) and embedded simulation faculty (n = 6). Results: From this, we built six interconnected themes: (1) simulation design: considered to optimise CoRL, (2) psychological safety: supports CoRL, (3) student agency and vicarious learning, (4) variable between simulation phases (pre-brief, task, debrief), (5) roles and role modelling: impact on CoRL and (6) learning conversations for CoRL. CoRL was described as most prevalent during task performance, indicating substantial learning occurs within the simulation itself, not just during the debrief. Educators can leverage this through SBE by using approaches such as “pause and discuss”. Learner agency was identified as a critical pre-requisite to CoRL, valued by both students and educators. Educators sought opportunities for students to exhibit their abilities, thereby fostering agency and creating openings for CoRL. Discussion: While generally beneficial, CoRL can sometimes manifest in unhelpful ways. This necessitates educator intervention (through role modelling or direct correction) and requires carefully balancing supporting students while still promoting self-regulated learning. We offer practical suggestions for health profession educators seeking to harness the benefits of CoRL in SBE to enhance collaborative learning and prepare future health professionals to be lifelong learners.

candidates.title: Drivers of advisory chatbot adoption in smallholder agriculture: A MICMAC analysis of farmer intermediary perceptions in the Sundarbans, India
candidates.abstract: In low-literacy, climate-vulnerable agricultural settings, smallholder farmers rarely evaluate new technologies independently; adoption is mediated through trusted institutional intermediaries. However, the systemic factors driving intermediary-perceived adoption of AI advisory tools remain unmapped. This study applies the Matrice d'Impacts Croisés-Multiplication Appliquée à un Classement (MICMAC) method to examine the systemic drivers of the adoption of generative AI-based agricultural chatbot s , namely, Krishi Dishari, based on the responses of thirty Gram Unnayan Karmi (GUK) intermediaries in the Sundarbans, India, a region facing salinity intrusion and extreme climate challenges. Using a structured bilingual influence matrix survey, the study mapped and classified twelve socio-technical variables by their driving and dependence power. The results indicate that institutional trust is a critical systemic linkage variable, with smartphone access serving as the primary technical driver and social learning emerging as the dominant diffusion mechanism. Furthermore, native language comfort (Bengali) emerged as a key transmission driver, confirming that linguistic accessibility is a prerequisite rather than an enhancement for technology adoption in low digital-literacy contexts. Consequently, this study offers a framework, although transferability warrants exhaustive validation, indicating that AI-based advisory services in vulnerable agricultural settings depend on institutional trust and social learning, not only on technological innovation.

candidates.title: Understanding workplace peer support among healthcare assistants providing palliative and end-of-life care at home: a realist review
candidates.abstract: Background: Healthcare assistants delivering home-based palliative and end-of-life care face complex emotional and clinical demands with limited workplace support. Peer support had been suggested as a potential solution, yet no reviews of such interventions exist. Aim: To understand and explain how, why, for whom and in what contexts workplace peer support interventions for healthcare assistants work (or do not work) in palliative and end-of-life care delivery at home. Design: Realist review registered with PROSPERO (registration number CRD42024606133). Data sources: CINAHL, MEDLINE, AMED, Scopus and grey literature with no date restrictions. Searches undertaken November-December 2024. All study designs containing data relevant to programme theory were included. Evidence was assessed for relevance, trustworthiness and rigour. Results: Synthesis of 24 sources from six countries generated 12 context-intervention-mechanism-outcome configurations used to develop initial programme theory. Four workforce outcomes of intervention include: enhanced wellbeing and resilience, reduced loneliness and isolation, development of a sense of community of practice and strengthened role identity. Three intervention strategies: peer-facilitated group meetings, 24/7 peer support access, and informal peer mentorship, create psychologically safe spaces, where individuals feel validated, valued, connected with others, enabling social learning. The intervention elements align with the fulfilment of three basic psychological needs: competence, autonomy, and relatedness. Conclusions: The initial programme theory reveals peer support may address core workforce challenges through psychologically safe peer connections and social learning, aligning with fulfilment of basic psychological needs. It provides a foundation for designing and testing evidence-informed peer support interventions for this workforce.

candidates.title: How Is Farmer Cooperation Possible? Interaction, Identity, and Community Capacity in a Chinese Rural Community
candidates.abstract: ABSTRACT How can cooperation emerge in communities where institutional enforcement is weak and social relations are fragmented? Drawing on a longitudinal case study of Village L in rural China (2017–2021), this paper develops a five‐stage process model that explains the endogenous emergence of cooperation. Moving beyond incentive‐ and institution‐centered accounts, the analysis shows how cooperation is dynamically generated through a sequence of interactional mechanisms: initiated by exemplary action, expanded through observational learning and symbolic reinforcement, deepened through deliberative coordination that activates a collective identity, and stabilized through ritualization into a cooperative cultural structure. The study demonstrates that farmers' agency is not a pregiven individual capacity but an emergent, relational outcome of interactional processes unfolding over time. By examining how interaction, identity formation, and cultural stabilization are linked in practice, this article treats cooperation as an emergent social accomplishment rather than a fixed equilibrium or a problem of institutional design. It develops a process‐based explanation of how community capacity and collective agency are gradually built in rural settings marked by weak institutions and fragmented social relations. In doing so, the study speaks to ongoing debates in rural sociology about how cooperation is generated and sustained in everyday social life.

candidates.title: How negative parenting relates to adolescents’ perceptions of older adults: the roles of empathy and intergenerational contact
candidates.abstract: Introduction Grounded in social learning theory, this study examines how negative parenting practices are associated with adolescents’ perceptions of older adults and investigates the roles of empathy and intergenerational contact in this process. Methods Data were collected from 2,011 Chinese adolescents using a three-wave longitudinal design. Structural equation modeling was used to test the hypothesized relationships. Results Negative parenting was significantly associated with less favorable evaluations of older adults on both the warmth and competence dimensions. Empathy mediated these relationships. Intergenerational contact further moderated the association between empathy and adolescents’ perceptions of older adults. Specifically, the indirect effects of negative parenting through empathy varied according to adolescents’ levels of intergenerational contact. Discussion These findings highlight family socialization as an important developmental context for adolescents’ perceptions of older adults and identify empathy as a key socio-emotional mechanism linking parenting experiences to intergenerational cognition.

candidates.title: Media's Role in Shaping Gender Norms and Perceptions: A Conceptual Review
candidates.venue: Budapest International Research and Critics Institute  (BIRCI-Journal): Humanities and Social Sciences
candidates.abstract: This study examines the role of media in shaping gender norms and perceptions, with particular attention to how media representations construct, reinforce, negotiate, and potentially transform understandings of masculinity and femininity. The study adopts a qualitative secondary-data approach, drawing on existing scholarly literature, empirical studies, theoretical perspectives, and documented evidence on gender representation across social media, with particular consideration of the Nigerian media context. The study argues that media should not be understood as a passive reflection of existing social realities but as an active cultural institution that participates in the construction and circulation of gender meanings. The reviewed evidence indicates that women continue to be disproportionately represented through appearance, domesticity, caregiving, emotionality, and subordinate roles, while men are frequently associated with authority, economic success, independence, dominance, and emotional restraint. Such recurring representations can normalise restrictive gender expectations through processes of observational learning and cumulative media exposure. In the Nigerian context, existing evidence suggests that gendered patterns identified in international scholarship are also evident in Nollywood and other media forms, although audiences interpret these representations through culturally specific frameworks. The study concludes that media remains a significant force in shaping gender perceptions, but its influence can also be mobilised for social transformation. Achieving more equitable gender perceptions therefore requires media representations that move beyond visibility towards diverse, meaningful, and non-stereotypical portrayals of women and men.

candidates.title: Cognitive and non-cognitive developmental outcomes in age-homogeneous and age-heterogeneous preschool classrooms: a systematic review
candidates.venue: European Early Childhood Education Research Journal
candidates.abstract: Age composition in pre-primary education, that is, the degree of age homogeneity or heterogeneity within classrooms, is one structural factor that may influence children's developmental outcomes. This systematic review, conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines, synthesises evidence from 23 empirical studies selected from 629 screened records. Studies were organised into two analytical domains: (1) cognitive outcomes and (2) noncognitive outcomes, the latter including natural school- or childcare-based studies and supplementary dyadic or controlled peer-interaction studies. Findings on cognitive outcomes are inconclusive. Some studies indicate modest advantages of age-homogeneous classrooms in selected domains, particularly preliteracy, early numeracy, executive functions and school readiness, but these effects are inconsistent and appear to depend on study design, outcome measures, instructional context and operationalisation of age composition. Findings on noncognitive outcomes more consistently suggest potential benefits of age-heterogeneous settings, particularly for peer interaction, social participation, cooperation, helping, role differentiation and observational learning. However, these findings require cautious interpretation because of methodological heterogeneity and the inclusion of dyadic or small-scale studies. Overall, age heterogeneity should be understood not as an independent causal factor, but as a structural condition that may create opportunities for peer-mediated learning and social interaction under specific pedagogical and organisational conditions.

candidates.title: It is time to revisit the external determinants of state terror
candidates.abstract: Authoritarian regimes are frequently influenced by external policies and transnational relationships when shaping domestic repression strategies. Existing empirical research has largely focused on demonstration and diffusion effects, emphasizing how governments emulate repressive practices observed abroad. Similarly, recent scholarship on authoritarian cooperation and regional organizations has argued that interstate cooperation strengthens authoritarian rule and facilitates repression through exchanges of information, expertise, resources, and strategic support. We distinguished theoretically between observational diffusion and cooperative interaction and examine empirically how each shapes state terror. Using spatial autoregressive combined models and global data on authoritarian regimes from 1947 to 2010, we found that demonstration via observational diffusion among institutionally similar regimes is generally associated with higher levels of state terror, whereas contemporaneous interdependence among such regimes is associated with lower levels. These results are broadly consistent across different specifications of the dependent variable. Our findings suggest a more nuanced relationship between interstate cooperation and repression: Cooperation may enhance authoritarian control while reducing reliance on the most extreme forms of violence. More broadly, the results indicate that diffusion-centered approaches may conflate observational learning with broader forms of authoritarian interdependence, thereby mischaracterizing the consequences of external influence for state terror.

candidates.title: Developing Gender Effective Coaches: Addressing the Knowledge to Application Gap
candidates.abstract: In recent years, there has been an increase in opportunities for women and girls in sport in Canada. Yet, biases, stereotypes, and norms about gender remain deeply embedded within sport culture (Goorevich & LaVoi, 2025), affecting girls and women across the landscape. The purpose of this doctoral dissertation was to provide coaches with evidence-based tools for their pursuit of gaining confidence in addressing and deconstructing gender beliefs that affect their coaching practice through three interconnected studies. The studies included: (1) the narrative exploration of gender beliefs and the impact they have on coaching methodologies, athlete interactions, and self-confidence; (2) the creation of a gender-related coaching self-efficacy scale; and (3) the exploration of coaches' knowledge-to-action processes through the lens of social learning. In this pursuit, I aimed to support coaches in their development of gender responsive and transformative practices to better address the needs of girls in sport. A pragmatic philosophical orientation, informed epistemologically by social constructionism, was used in this dissertation research. In line with pragmatism, a mixed methods design approach was executed taking into consideration four theoretical frameworks including a combined model of coach self-efficacy (Feltz et al., 1999) and coach effectiveness (Horn, 2002; 2008; Côté & Gilbert, 2009), Wenger's (1998) theory of social learning and communities of practice, and Goorevich and LaVoi's (2025) continuum of gendered sport coach discourses. The results of this inquiry are presented through three articles. In the first study, entirely qualitative in nature, I present composite vignettes that explored the diverse and context-dependent experiences of coaches coaching girls, further nuanced by the lived realities of women coaches. Data collection consisted of focus groups with 20 coaches ranging in sport and coaching experience. This narrative inquiry aims to illustrate how coaching philosophies and practices are socially shaped through gendered discourses operating within sport. As a result of the findings from this examination, potential items for the scale development study were created. The need for more opportunities for coaches to develop self-awareness regarding their gender biases, reflect, and deconstruct their gender beliefs to make changes to their coaching practices was also highlighted as future areas for growth in coach education. The second study was conducted through a mixed methods approach, consisting of the development and primary validation of the Girls-Centred Coaching Self-Efficacy Scale (GCSES). The scale development process followed previously established methodological guidelines (i.e., Boateng et al., 2018) with an initial 87 items being created through theory-driven item construction, coach focus groups (n = 20), expert review (n = 6), and cognitive interviews with coaches (n = 4). The revised instrument after this process included 31 items and was administered to 216 sport coaches. An exploratory factor analysis supported a four-factor structure for 23 final items accounting for 54.9% of the variance with strong internal consistency across subscales (⍺ = .80-.92). Subscales include: (1) gender literacy in coaching, (2) understanding gendered sport experiences, (3) fostering gender-inclusive sport, and (4) girl-centred coaching practices. The findings from this study provide evidence for the GCSES to be used as a context-specific tool for evaluations and interventions aimed at advancing gender responsive and transformative coaching practices. The third study used a mixed methods quasi-experimental design, exploring coaches' knowledge-to-action processes related to their girl-centred coaching self-efficacy through a combined online and social learning intervention. Twenty-five coaches took part in one of two conditions over a five-month period, either completing the series of Coaching HER's foundational eLearning modules by themselves or engaging in a community of practice (CoP; Wenger, 1998) concurrent with the eLearning modules. Coaches in both groups took the GCSES pre- and post-intervention, and data were analyzed using mixed ANOVAs. Participants in the CoP condition were also invited to partake in a focus group (n = 6) grounded in the value creation framework (VCF; Wenger-Trayner & Wenger-Trayner, 2020) to explore how value was created through their participation in the CoP. Effect and contribution data were collected throughout the intervention period (Wenger-Trayner et al., 2019). Although the study was underpowered to detect statistically significant differences between conditions, coaches who engaged in the CoP condition demonstrated small trends of mean improvements across all GCSES factors compared to the eLearning condition. Qualitative data, presented through two value creation stories (VCSs; Wenger-Trayner et al., 2019) and individual value cycle examples, aided in providing insight into the GCSES results as well as how coaches in the CoP condition translated learnings into changes to their practices. Altogether, the findings from the final study in this dissertation suggested that engagement in a CoP fostered opportunities for self-reflection, accountability, and contextual application of knowledge. Recommendations included the continued use of social learning in tandem with eLearning for coaching education to better support coaches' knowledge-to-action processes and the value of mixed methods research in this domain. The results of this doctoral dissertation aim to provide an evidence-based foundation for understanding, measuring, and supporting coaches' development toward more girl-centred and gender-equitable coaching practices. Collectively, the findings advance both theory and practice by offering practical tools, empirical evidence, and a conceptual framework to guide future coach education, research, and organizational efforts aimed at fostering meaningful and sustainable gender equity in sport.

candidates.title: Preventing Employee Fraud Through Ethical Culture: Addressing Rationalisation in the Fraud Triangle
candidates.venue: International Journal of Applied Research in Business and Management
candidates.abstract: Employee fraud represents a persistent challenge for organisations worldwide, with significant financial and reputational consequences. This article synthesises findings from 25 peer-reviewed studies to examine how ethical culture functions as a primary mechanism for preventing occupational fraud, with particular attention to disrupting the rationalisation element of the fraud triangle. Through a systematic analysis of empirical research published between 2022 and 2025, this study identifies the mechanisms by which ethical culture undermines employees' ability to justify fraudulent behaviour. The reviewed studies suggest that comprehensive ethical culture interventions, including leadership commitment, ethics training, whistleblowing systems, and accountability structures, are associated with reductions in reported fraud incidence by addressing all three components of the fraud triangle, particularly rationalisation. This article contributes to fraud prevention literature by providing an integrated framework, combining Fraud Triangle Theory, Ethical Climate Theory, and Social Learning Theory, with a specific focus on rationalisation and on organisational moral disengagement as a mediating mechanism, for understanding how ethical culture interrupts the psychological and organisational processes that enable employee fraud. Practical implications for organisations seeking to strengthen their anti-fraud cultural infrastructure are discussed.

candidates.title: BEYOND INTERNAL VS. EXTERNAL TRAINING: DESIGNING HYBRID LEARNING ARCHITECTURES FOR COLLECTIVE LEARNING
candidates.abstract: This conceptual paper reconceptualizes organizational training systems as learning architectures that shape how learning is generated, transferred, and institutionalized. Rather than treating training as a mere operational activity, it is positioned as a strategic learning capability influencing long-term organizational adaptability. The analysis demonstrates that internal cascade and external training architectures support distinct learning dynamics. Cascade systems strengthen contextualization and social learning but risk knowledge dilution, whereas external training enhances exploratory learning but often lacks mechanisms for sustained integration. To address these limitations, the study develops a hybrid training architecture that combines external knowledge infusion with internally embedded routines, supporting both innovation and learning continuity. While lacking empirical testing , this framework provides a theoretical foundation for future research on how training architectures influence learning processes across different contexts. Practically, it offers leaders a conceptually grounded guide for selecting training models based on learning objectives and environmental volatility, encouraging a shift from cost-driven to learning-oriented design. Ultimately, this paper advances learning organization scholarship by linking training system design to capability renewal and long-term adaptability.

candidates.title: When groups attract: coevolutionary dynamics of cooperation and individual- and group-based imitating rules
candidates.abstract: Success-driven imitation is a fundamental aspect of social learning, yet group interactions beyond pairwise require more subtle imitating rules since success can be observed at either the group or individual level. How such heuristic imitating rules based on these distinct levels of social information compete and coevolve with collective behavior, particularly cooperation, remains poorly understood. Here, we address this issue by studying the coevolutionary dynamics of cooperation in public goods games and individual- and group-based imitating rules on hypergraphs. We distinguish three rules according to whether payoff-biased imitation operates at the individual level, the group level, or both. Our results identify a mutual reinforcement between cooperation and group-biased imitation: preferentially learning from successful groups promotes cooperation, while cooperators in turn favor group-biased imitation. We confirm this synergy between cooperation and group-biased imitation across diverse synthetic and empirical higher-order network populations. We further show that the subtle scale and organization of group interactions critically shape this coevolution, with intermediate group sizes providing the greatest advantage for cooperation. Our results reveal how learning whom to imitate can jointly evolve to shape collective cooperation.

candidates.title: “Crack,” the Fog of Disorder, and Congressional Leadership in the War on Drugs: The Political Development of the Anti-Drug Abuse Act of 1986
candidates.abstract: Abstract This article traces the development of the Anti-Drug Abuse Act of 1986, arguing that its punitive structure emerged less from ideological design or presidential strategy than from congressional policymaking under conditions of extreme uncertainty—what this study terms the fog of disorder . While existing scholarship emphasizes moral panic or Reagan-era racial politics, this analysis shifts attention to Congress itself. Drawing on archival research from nearly 30 collections—including presidential papers, municipal records, and the personal archives of roughly 20 members of Congress—the article shows how lawmakers confronted crack cocaine as a novel and poorly understood phenomenon characterized by fragmented information, escalating fear, and electoral pressure. In this environment, congressional leaders acted as policy entrepreneurs, using omnibus legislation and compressed procedures to force action and sustain fragile coalitions despite limited evidence. Finally, the article shows how the accumulation of new information through policy implementation—especially evidence of racial disparity and lived experiences with punishment—eventually generated social learning, interest mobilization, and reform. By centering uncertainty, information, and institutional venue and strategy, this study explains both the origins of draconian policy designs and the pathways through which they were later challenged and revised.

candidates.title: Behind closed doors: access to dissecting rooms in the UK
candidates.abstract: This study presents an analysis of the factors that affect anatomists' decisions around which occupations they would allow to access dissection and dissection rooms in the UK. Whilst participation, or observation, of dissection of a donated human body is a foundational element of most medical education in the UK, other occupations that work with the human body are often precluded from accessing such facilities. The research involved interviewing 30 anatomists, representing over 70% of UK medical schools with a body donation programme. These semi-structured interviews were transcribed, encoded, and subjected to thematic analysis to explore the criteria for excluding certain professions from dissection activities. From the data collected I examine which of 12 occupations (Radiographers, Physiotherapists, Dentists, Nurses, Medical Students, Midwives, Massage Therapists, Osteopaths/Chiropractors, Exercise Professionals, Reflexologists/Acupuncturists, Artists, and Botox Injectors) would be granted access by my interviewees to their hypothetical ideal dissection facility, and whether these occupations would be allowed to participate actively in dissections or would be restricted to observational learning through models and prosections. The analysis also addresses the reasons the anatomists gave for any restrictions, linking their decisions to sociological theories of boundary work, identity development, and occupational demarcation. From the interview data I demonstrate that in an arena where the epistemic and educational value of human dissection is debated, the anatomists' concern is that granting access to occupations they believe to be less widely respected might lead to their own reputational loss. The anatomists believe that this reputational loss would affect donor numbers which would affect their ability to continue to teach by dissection, jeopardising their already diminishing position within medical education. They mitigate this reputational loss by creating boundaries around the act and location of dissection that limit who can access the resources.

candidates.title: Exploring the perceived contribution of non-subject co-curricular clubs to students’ moral behaviour in selected secondary schools in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania: A multiple-case study
candidates.abstract: This study examined how non-subject co-curricular clubs influence moral behaviour among secondary school students in Dar es Salaam. It examined club types, objectives, behavioural impacts, and factors affecting effectiveness, using a qualitative case study conducted from 1 June to 10 August 2026. Guided by Social Learning Theory, the study used this as the primary interpretive framework, complemented by Dewey’s experiential perspective and Bronfenbrenner’s ecological view of behaviour. Data were collected between 1 June and 10 August 2026 through four focus group discussions involving 24 students (six per school) and eight semi-structured individual interviews with four teachers and four club patrons/matrons. The 12 transcripts from 32 participants were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis, including within-case and cross-case comparisons. Analysis revealed that schools had a broad ecology of clubs, but formal availability often exceeded regular functionality. Participants linked activities to values such as respect, responsibility, honesty, cooperation, self-discipline, and confidence, but factors such as passive delivery, uneven participation, and external influences limited their impact. Challenges included timetable conflicts, exam pressure, teacher workload, lack of supervision, guidance, resources, external support, and motivation. The study concludes that clubs can positively reinforce moral learning, but their effects are conditional rather than causal. Recommendations include allocated time, proper audits, training, resources, student leadership, inclusive participation, stronger partnerships, and behaviour monitoring.

candidates.title: The Internalization of Inclusive and Adaptive Values in Bullying Prevention Among Students at Girls’ Islamic Boarding School
candidates.abstract: Bullying remains a concern in Islamic boarding schools (pesantren), where intensive residential interactions may create complex social dynamics among students. This study aims to identify the inclusive and adaptive values developed at Al-Ishlahiyyah Girls’ Islamic Boarding School, Wonorejo, East Java, Indonesia, examine how these values are internalized through everyday educational and social practices, and analyze their contribution to bullying prevention. A qualitative approach with an intrinsic case study design was employed. Data were collected through participant observation, semi-structured interviews, and document analysis involving the boarding school caregiver, ustadzah, dormitory supervisors, senior students, and junior students. Data were analyzed through data reduction, data display, and conclusion drawing and verification, supported by source triangulation, method triangulation, and an audit trail. The findings identified four interrelated values: tolerance, empathy, equality, and social justice. These values were internalized through four interconnected mechanisms: modeling, habituation, mentoring, and institutional policy structures. The findings further indicate that these mechanisms were associated with more inclusive verbal interactions, reduced relational exclusion, greater psychological and emotional security, and a reorientation of senior–junior relations from domination toward guidance and support. Drawing on social learning theory, the study demonstrates that bullying prevention may be understood as a socio-cultural process in which values are learned, reinforced, and enacted through everyday interactions and institutional practices. The study contributes a context-sensitive perspective on value internalization as a preventive dimension of bullying in girls’ Islamic boarding schools

candidates.title: Co-offending roles, training, and progression through the ranks
candidates.abstract: This chapter examines co-offending as a dynamic social process through which children acquire criminal skills, roles, and status and may become vulnerable to more organised and exploitative contexts. Integrating Bronfenbrenner’s ecological systems theory with contextual safeguarding, routine activities theory, rational choice theory, and social learning theory, it conceptualises group offending as shaped by developmental susceptibility to peer influence, opportunity structures, and learnt definitions that normalise risk-taking. Building on research showing that co-offending roles are fluid, it explains how adolescents move among instigator, equal-role, and follower positions as group composition, perceived rewards, and situational conditions evolve. Findings are organised across two interlinked networks. Figure 2.1 (see also Table 2.1 for associated quotations) maps crime strategies and roles, distinguishing impulsive/opportunistic acts from planned offences and illustrating escalation within events and over time. Figure 2.2 traces training processes, including peer instruction, mentoring by older individuals (family and community adults), and self-training via experimentation and reinforcement. Participant accounts show how initially positive perceptions of mentors can later be reframed as manipulation, as children recognise heightened exposure to violence and instrumental use by others. The chapter concludes with practice implications, emphasising early, context-sensitive interventions that disrupt harmful peer and adult influence, support prosocial identity development, and provide credible routes to status and income outside offending.

candidates.title: Selective Epistemic Trust and the Recovery of Agency After Interpersonal Trauma
candidates.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
candidates.abstract: Interpersonal trauma can disturb how people evaluate communicated information, yet greater willingness to accept advice is an ambiguous marker of psychological recovery. A person may become more receptive to useful guidance while also becoming less able to question unreliable authority. This critical integrative review examines whether selective epistemic trust offers a more defensible clinical objective than increasing trust alone. Targeted searches of biomedical records, publisher resources, and relevant reference lists informed a synthesis of developmental theory, psychometric research, psychotherapy process studies, and scholarship on epistemic injustice. The evidence supports distinguishing trust, mistrust, and credulity, but associations with symptoms vary across instruments and populations. Recent behavioural and observational studies extend assessment beyond self-report, although they do not establish that increasing advice acceptance causes recovery after trauma. The article develops an evaluative framework connecting sensitivity to information quality with the patient's capacity to question, revise, and retain ownership of decisions. Its central proposition is that therapeutic benefit should include learning from credible communication without making agreement with the clinician the criterion of improvement. A proposed research programme separates source reliability, emotional safety, prior confidence, and the consequences of error; combines repeated behavioural assessment with session observation and patient-defined outcomes; and tests whether changes generalise beyond the treatment relationship. Competing explanations include symptom relief, alliance quality, task familiarity, and accommodation to authority. Selective trust remains a candidate process requiring prospective validation. Its immediate contribution is to clarify what successful social learning should preserve: openness to evidence together with meaningful authorship of personal choices.

candidates.title: Rotating Class Routines Foster Mutual Cooperation In Early Childhood Civic Education
candidates.venue: Indonesian Journal of Education Methods Development
candidates.abstract: General Background Civic instruction serves a fundamental function in shaping foundational character traits and social habits among young children. Specific Background The second-grade demographic at SDN Sinar Jaya consists of only three individuals, presenting a unique classroom dynamic that requires specific pedagogical adaptation. Knowledge Gap Moral theories taught in schools frequently remain abstract, lacking direct habituation mechanisms that convert theoretical citizenship concepts into tangible, daily collective actions. Aims This implementation seeks to instill shared responsibility and mutual assistance through the execution of a daily scheduled task rotation. Results Observational evaluations indicated that participants successfully completed assigned physical chores, such as sweeping and arranging chairs, achieving high assessment scores between 12 and 13. Additionally, participants demonstrated spontaneous initiative by voluntarily aiding peers who encountered difficulties during their respective assignments. Novelty Leveraging a micro-group environment enables highly intensive teacher mentoring, converting basic classroom maintenance into a deeply personalized pedagogical instrument for character formation. Implications Embedding scheduled practical activities within daily educational schedules offers teachers an actionable strategy to ensure abstract social values materialize as permanent behavioral traits. Highlights: Scheduled physical chores successfully transformed abstract moral theories into concrete daily actions. Observational assessments revealed high participant compliance and excellent micro-group performance metrics. Personalized teacher guidance triggered spontaneous peer assistance and shared responsibility among learners. Keywords: Character Building, Habituation Method, Social Learning, Shared Responsibility, Micro Cohort

candidates.title: Documentation of co-creation and data supporting the development of a serious game for social skills
candidates.abstract: Abstract Adolescence is a critical period for the maturation of brain regions underlying social cognition, such as socio-moral reasoning (SMR) and decision-making. Adolescents—and adults who work with them—should have access to validated pedagogical tools and effective resources to support their social learning during this period. These tools are especially important when social or affective deficits are identified, given these can lead to maladaptive behaviors or mental health problems. However, few learning or intervention tools aimed at improving socio-moral reasoning and decision-making exist. The design of such tools should consider factors related to validity and youth engagement to ensure uptake and thus requires a break from traditional approaches. In response to this challenge, the Are you GAME? project aims to develop a serious video game (i.e., an interactive digital game designed for purposes beyond entertainment) designed to target socio-moral reasoning and decision-making abilities in adolescents. We present findings from four recherche-creation phases (Gamestorm session, Focus groups with adolescents, Focus groups with educators, Playtests) involving diverse co-creation partners (researchers, industry partners, user groups) to ensure transparency, support reproducibility, and inform future work in serious game design. The research-creation process comprised 15 co-creation sessions involving 72 participants, including adolescents, educators, researchers, and game design professionals. Qualitative data consisting of field notes, audio recordings, and written reports were analyzed through documentation across successive research-creation cycles. Preliminary Playtest results indicate that the game is a promising tool for promoting youth social competence.

candidates.title: Enhancing smallholder farmers’ willingness to adopt organic fertilizer in Zhejiang Province, China: a configurational analysis of pathways
candidates.abstract: Scope Organic fertilizer substitution can reduce agricultural non-point source pollution, but subsidy programs in China often exclude smallholder farmers. This study evaluates the effectiveness and feasibility of subsidizing smallholders in Zhejiang Province and identifies combinations of internal factors associated with their willingness to adopt organic fertilizer substitution. Methods Data were obtained from 288 smallholder farmers in 11 green agricultural pioneer counties. The contingent valuation method and willingness to accept were used to estimate expected subsidy levels under different substitution ratios. The theory of planned behavior and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis were then integrated to examine six internal conditions: ecological rationality, economic rationality, exemplary norms, directive norms, competence perception, and policy perception. Results Subsidies increased stated willingness, and the estimated willingness to accept was generally below prevailing subsidy levels. At a 40–60% substitution ratio, the expected subsidy was 124.74 Chinese yuan per metric ton. No single internal condition was necessary for high willingness. Instead, six configurations formed four pathways: Learning, External Normative, Resource-oriented, and Benefit-oriented. These pathways show that technical learning and competence, institutional and peer influence, access to on-farm organic resources, and perceived economic and ecological benefits operate in different combinations across heterogeneous smallholders. Perspectives Policy should (1) implement tiered subsidies according to farm scale and substitution needs, (2) refine agricultural technology extension by combining accessible training with online and offline communication, and (3) strengthen social learning through peer demonstration and locally trusted information channels. The configurational approach offers a differentiated basis for promoting organic fertilizer substitution in comparable smallholder regions.

candidates.title: Supporting managers’ emotion regulation in virtual leadership: a qualitative study of HRD and workplace learning conditions
candidates.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how workplace learning and human resource development (HRD) conditions shape managers’ emotion regulation (ER) capacity in virtual leadership. Rather than treating ER as a stable individual competence, it focuses on workplace learning processes and organizational support through which managers develop and sustain ER capacity. Design/methodology/approach This study draws on 45 semistructured interviews conducted in Germany in 2022 with managers who had led employees virtually or in hybrid settings during the pandemic period. It uses abductive qualitative content analysis, with job demands-resources theory as the primary organizing framework, workplace learning/HRD as the developmental perspective and affordance theory as a supporting lens. Findings The findings show that virtual leadership creates reduced emotional observability, making it harder for managers to perceive mood, strain and relational tension. Managers’ ER capacity was shaped by organizational resources such as trust, autonomy and cultural permission, while HRD support varied considerably. Reflective and social learning spaces emerged as a developmental condition. The study also identifies ambivalent emotional affordances: virtual work can reduce cues and create distance but can also enable safety, disclosure and new forms of closeness. Practical implications The findings suggest that organizations consider a broader organizational approach extending beyond individual resilience training, including senior leadership commitment, integrated HRD, peer reflection, communication norms and workload-sensitive well-being practices. Originality/value The paper’s main integrative contribution is emotional development infrastructure, connecting organizational conditions, HRD practices, learning spaces and work design in shaping managers’ ER capacity. Reduced emotional observability and ambivalent emotional affordances provide complementary empirical contributions.

candidates.title: The Impact of Social Media Algorithms on Religious Belief Formation and Community Engagement
candidates.venue: JOURNAL OF HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL POLICY
candidates.abstract: This study explores how social media algorithms influence the growth of religious beliefs and community involvement in today's digital landscape. As platforms like Facebook, YouTube, Instagram, and TikTok increasingly suggest religious content through their algorithms, the way people make meaning of their faith is shaped not only by traditional religious institutions or personal decisions but also by data-driven personalization. Combining insights from social learning theory and mediated religion theory, the research takes an interdisciplinary approach, blending ideas from computer science and religious studies to examine both individual beliefs and collective religious interactions online. Data gathered from surveys of 400 active social media users and analysis of religious posts recommended by algorithms across major platforms reveal that these algorithms significantly affect exposure to religious ideas, reinforcing familiar themes and beliefs through repeated visibility. Many users reported that amplified algorithmic content influences their understanding of religious teachings and of what they consider credible beliefs. The findings also suggest that social media algorithms encourage religious community involvement by fostering virtual connections, promoting discussions, and strengthening a sense of belonging that complements offline religious practices. Additionally, the study notes a shift in religious authority, where metrics like likes, shares, and followers increasingly influence trust and credibility, sometimes more than traditional institutional or doctrinal authority. Despite being aware of algorithmic control, users still rely heavily on social media for religious learning, highlighting that awareness alone doesn’t fully mitigate algorithmic influence. Overall, the research indicates that while algorithms open new doors for religious engagement and community building, they also pose ethical and epistemological questions about authority, diversity, and the potential for beliefs to become more uniform. In summary, the study emphasizes the importance of digital religious literacy and ongoing interdisciplinary research to better understand how algorithms shape religious life in the digital age.

candidates.title: Adolescent smoking and social norms: an appraisal of theory and application of social norms to understand risk factors for smoking and sensitivity to normative influence
candidates.abstract: Background: As a developmental period, adolescence is critical for the formation of health behaviours that are carried into adulthood. The social reorientation that occurs during adolescence marks an important stage in development when normative influences become more salient, and social pressures to conform to the behaviours of peers increase in their magnitude and regularity. One behavioural outcome that is examined consistently in the literature is smoking, the social antecedents of which are well-documented and have been explored using a range of different theoretical models which are explored in Chapter 2. While social norms are important determinants of smoking behaviour, they are not universal across all contexts. For example, in low-middle-income countries tobacco advertising is more prominent and smoke-free regulatory frameworks are not consistently implemented. As a result, the global burden of tobacco-related disease has shifted to low-middle-income settings where the tobacco industry can circumvent local tobacco legislation with relatively little resistance. By comparison, smoking rates in high-income countries are significantly lower and Chapter 3 investigated how the factors that contribute to smoking differ across these contexts. Despite a large body of research delineating the normative and psychosocial antecedents of adolescent behaviour, there are few studies that have attempted to expound upon the specific personality and cognitive traits that make adolescents more susceptible to normative influence. Therefore, the objective of Chapter 4 was to explore the psychosocial and cognitive traits associated with sensitivity to social norms using a novel experimental tool designed to gauge adolescent’s norms sensitivity using a modified version of a rule-following task. Method: Chapter 2 is a theory landscaping review (supported by systematic methodological elements) of studies that utilise theoretical models to examine the role of social influence in adolescent smoking. The analytical framework was grounded in a meta-narrative framework that utilised a model of theory synthesis proposed by Pound and Campbell. This facilitated the identification of key themes and commonalities within the literature and presents a narrative overview of how theoretical models have been applied to understand the contribution of social influence to adolescent smoking. To visually illustrate the overlap in measures of social influence used in the studies, a hierarchical edge bundling diagram was rendered using Vega data visualisation software. Chapters 3 and 4 employed baseline data collected during the Mechanisms of Networks and Norms Influence on Smoking in Schools (MECHANISMS) study. The MECHANISMS study was a school-based proof of concept study designed to further understanding of social norms based mechanisms of action related to smoking in high- and low-middle-income settings. Students in Northern Ireland and Bogotá, Colombia completed self-administered questionnaires measuring various normative, socio-environmental and psychosocial constructs related to smoking, as well as a series of Game Theory experiments designed to elicit individual sensitivity to norms. Chapter 3 is a cross-cultural comparison of the socio-environmental and psychosocial factors associated with smoking susceptibility among adolescents from two settings with contrasting sociocultural characteristics. Logistic regression analysis was used to examine how these predictors of smoking susceptibility compared across the two countries. Chapter 4 investigated the association between norms sensitivity and a number of personality and cognitive traits, and to understand if these associations varied according to gender. A series of multilevel linear mixed effects models and ordered logistic regression models were employed to assess the association between sensitivity to norms and the personality and cognitive traits. The data were disaggregated by gender and the analyses performed separately for each group. Results: The results of Chapter 2 highlighted three theories that featured prominently in the studies reviewed: the Theory of Planned Behaviour; Social Cognitive / Social Learning Theory; and Ecological Systems Theory. The studies primarily used descriptive norms and sociocultural factors to gauge social influence. Other factors such as injunctive norms, parental monitoring and perceived pressure to smoke were also investigated with relative consistency. The results of Chapter 3 showed that the correlates of smoking susceptibility differed in their magnitude and distribution across the two settings. The results of Chapter 4 were consistent with the findings of an earlier study, identifying gender as the only factor that consistently demonstrated a significant association with sensitivity to norms. Conclusions: In Chapter 2, it was evident that a broad range of instruments, scales, and variables were used to capture ostensibly similar theoretical constructs that relate to social influence. Thus, a formal framework that unifies the multiple theoretical perspectives is needed to advance the scientific discourse around social influence and adolescent smoking. By comparing the risk factors for smoking susceptibility in settings with generally dissonant cultural and social properties, Chapter 3 highlighted the need for interventions targeting adolescent smoking to be sensitive to the unique sociocultural characteristics of the context within which they are implemented. The results of Chapter 4 suggested that sensitivity to norms is an independent, and stable, personality dimension. However, sensitivity to norms is still a relatively underexplored construct within the literature. As such, future research should attempt to capture sensitivity to different types of norms (i.e., injunctive norms, subjective norms, descriptive norms) and expand upon these findings to better understand the interaction between gender and norms sensitivity in adolescent decision-making. Chapter 5 expands upon some of the implications for future research, drawing attention to the role of social norms in designing effective smoking prevention interventions, and the implications associated with the emergence of e-cigarettes as an alternative to conventional cigarette smoking.

candidates.title: Procedural Reciprocity: Admitting Late Counterclaims in Arbitration
candidates.abstract: This article proposes a Structured Admissibility Test for counterclaims submitted after a claimant materially amends its case. It addresses an under-examined asymmetry in international commercial arbitration, particularly in disputes arising from commercial contracts: claimants may be permitted to reshape the dispute, while respondents remain subject to deadlines established by reference to the original claims. The article conceptualizes procedural reciprocity as a functional application of equality of arms to the allocation of procedural opportunities in evolving proceedings. It does not treat a material amendment as creating an automatic right to counterclaim. Rather, the amendment may justify consideration of a genuinely responsive counterclaim that falls within the parties’ existing consent to arbitration. The analysis distinguishes the tribunal’s jurisdiction, which derives from consent, from the evolving scope of the dispute submitted for determination. A comparison of the UNCITRAL, ICC, SIAC, and LCIA frameworks shows that contemporary rules confer sufficient flexibility but provide limited guidance on its exercise. The proposed test requires tribunals to assess jurisdiction and consent, the causal justification for delay, respondent diligence, and whether prejudice can be cured through proportionate timetable and cost measures. The framework disciplines arbitral discretion, promotes procedural consistency, and reduces fragmented dispute resolution.

candidates.title: The ecological cost of retaliation bounds decentralised reciprocity in commons with tipping points
candidates.abstract: This project provides code for an N-player common-pool resource model with threshold regeneration, irreversible collapse, and aggregate monitoring. It computes theoretical viability bounds, certifies management rules against a defector’s best response, and examines rule discovery through multi-agent reinforcement learning and evolutionary dynamics. The study shows how harvesting-based retaliation can make unexploitability and ecological viability jointly unattainable.

candidates.title: Physiological synchrony predicts reduced reciprocity only in face-to-face interactions
candidates.venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B Biological Sciences
candidates.abstract: Across species, cooperative decisions are often asymmetric: one individual risks their own resources before knowing whether others will reciprocate. Such uncertainty is central to the evolution of trust and reciprocal exchanges. Physiological synchrony is frequently assumed to support cooperation, yet it remains unclear both how synchrony arises and how it functions in these asymmetric social interactions. We tested whether mutual visibility shapes physiological synchrony, and whether synchrony in turn predicts cooperative behaviour in repeated trust-reciprocity exchanges. Skin conductance synchrony was stronger and more temporally aligned when individuals interacted face-to-face, yet facial expressivity did not account for this effect. Contrary to the dominant perspective, higher synchrony predicted reduced reciprocity, and only when partners could see each other. Exploratory analyses suggested that this negative link depended on arousal, indicating that the social function of synchrony is shaped by both mutual visibility and the affective state of the individual involved. These findings show that physiological synchrony is not a uniformly prosocial mechanism but a context-dependent phenomenon that can undermine cooperation under certain conditions, offering insight into the mechanisms and the function of synchrony in shaping cooperative exchanges.

candidates.title: Witchcraft, trust, and reciprocity among Mozambican refugees and their South African hosts in a Lowveld village
candidates.abstract: Research on black African refugees and immigrants in South Africa has focused disproportionately on their experience in urban areas. We know a great deal about the harassment and harsh treatment they suffer at the hands of mainly black South Africans. We know very little of the experience of rural-based refugees and immigrants. Also, research about immigrants tends to focus on their experiences to the exclusion of the everyday lives of their hosts. In this paper I turn the spotlight on rural-based refugees in a South African village. In addition to examining their relationship with their hosts, I discuss relationships within the two communities and how they are shaped by internal factors such as belief in witchcraft, and external ones such as government policies and socio-economic circumstances. What emerges is a complex picture that challenges conventional wisdom about the attitude of South Africans towards immigrants and refugees, and about refugees as a problem.

candidates.title: Reciprocity Within the University: Grassroots Financial Aid as Hidden University–Community Engagement in a Global South Context
candidates.venue: Gateways International Journal of Community Research and Engagement
candidates.abstract: A grassroots financial aid initiative established in 2018 by lecturers in the Department of Accounting at Politeknik Negeri Ujung Pandang, Indonesia, emerged after several students experienced severe financial hardship, including food insecurity, that affected their ability to participate in classes. In response, lecturers voluntarily contributed a portion of their monthly salaries to establish a collective fund known as ‘bansos’ (social aid). Initially created to provide emergency assistance for students’ tuition fees and daily food needs, the fund gradually expanded to support Internet data packages during the COVID-­ 19 pandemic, and later, emergency assistance for cleaning staff and colleagues facing financial difficulties. The initiative operates through a simple, trust-­ based mechanism in which students experiencing financial hardship are identified by peers or academic advisors, screened by a coordinator and approved by the department. Assistance is provided without burdensome administrative requirements, enabling rapid responses to urgent needs. Sustained entirely through voluntary donations and mutual trust, the initiative has evolved into an informal departmental safety net that continues to support members of the university community experiencing financial hardship. The initiative contributes to understandings of university–­ community engagement (UCE) by advancing an expanded concept of community. Rather than viewing community solely as an external group or ‘outsider’ to the university, it demonstrates that community (in fact, sites of precarity and social vulnerability) can also exist and be engaged with within the university itself. This suggests that UCE is not always necessarily outward-­ facing. In this way, the initiative blurs the conventional boundary between university and community. The initiative also extends understandings of UCE beyond formal, programmatic partnerships. It foregrounds the often-invisible moral labour involved in responding to precarity, as well as the significance of micro-­ level engagement and embodied reciprocity. Situated in Indonesia, this Snapshot contributes to diversifying the narratives of UCE that have predominantly emerged from the Global North and highlights the significance of informal, relational and grassroots forms of engagement in the Global South.

candidates.title: Who gains, who decides? Trust, reciprocity, and power in luxury productization for community-based rural tourism

"Reciprocity" Is Four Theorems: Three Need Only Symmetry, One Needs Time Reversal ── reciprocity of a stiffness matrix rests on symmetry alone and breaks when it is made asymmetric, yet with a magnetic field, where the symmetry is gone, L(B) still equals the transpose of L(-B) ── one word, two different requirements ── [Paper 542]
candidates.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
candidates.abstract: Optics, electromagnetism, structural mechanics and thermodynamics each have a reciprocity theorem. What this paper shows is that the first three require only that an operator be symmetric, while the fourth requires reversing the sign of the magnetic field as well. No new theorem or law is claimed. Scope of this paper (scope note): No new theorem or law is claimed──the reciprocity relations of Helmholtz, Lorentz, Betti and Onsager are all standard. The Onsager relations are not proved──the derivation from microscopic reversibility is not entered; only the shape of the relation is examined numerically. No real material is treated──the matrices are illustrative and are not the coefficients of any substance. Nonlinear cases are not covered──only linear response is examined. No non-reciprocal device is designed──isolators and circulators are not the subject. It is not claimed that four exhausts the list──four were counted, and no more are asserted. Neither "the same theorem" nor "unrelated" is claimed──what is shared is a shape, and the requirements differ. Relation to earlier papers: Paper 143 showed that minimum entropy production is not a principle but a theorem with a fence──one part of that fence is the Onsager relation, and this paper shows that relation differs in shape from the other three. Paper 77 treated fine-grained conservation and coarse-grained growth──the time reversal the Onsager relation requires lives on the fine-grained side. Paper 125 showed that there are three Hopfs──this is likewise a census, of a word rather than a name, and it divides. Paper 300 showed that sharing a root is decidable──the four split three against one under the criterion of what a quantity carries. What is added is confirming numerically that symmetry gives exact reciprocity, measuring a relative break of 0.6667 when symmetry is removed, showing reciprocity surviving a destroyed symmetry under a magnetic field, restoring it by switching the field off, and placing the separator on the number of states required. First, with a symmetric operator reciprocity is exact──for a symmetric stiffness matrix the difference between f_1. u_2 and f_2. u_1 is 0.00x10^0 (Section 2). Second, making it asymmetric breaks it──a difference of 0.029851, relatively 0.6667: the far side of the boundary (Section 2). Third, and this is the core. With a magnetic field the symmetry is destroyed and reciprocity survives──|L_12-L_21|=1.600000, and yet L(B) matches the transpose of L(-B) with difference 0.00x10^0 (Section 3). Fourth, switching off the field restores ordinary symmetry──at B=0, |L_12-L_21| falls to the 10^-15 level (Section 3). Fifth, the conditions have different shapes──the first three can be stated about one matrix; the fourth needs two states, B and -B, set side by side (Section 4). Sixth, the separator is how many states are needed──one, or two (Section 4). Optics, electromagnetism, structural mechanics and thermodynamics each have a reciprocity theorem. Three need only a symmetric operator──with a symmetric stiffness matrix, f_1. u_2 and f_2. u_1 differ by 0.00x10^0, exactly zero rather than at the rounding level, so this is an identity. Making the matrix asymmetric opens a difference of 0.029851, relatively 0.6667, so reciprocity does not simply always hold. Optics and electromagnetism share the shape, since a reciprocal medium makes the operator symmetric, and what is required is one property of one operator. The fourth holds without symmetry──in a linear-response matrix with a term odd in the field, |L_12-L_21|=1.600000 destroys the symmetry, and yet L(B) matches the transpose of L(-B) with difference 0.00x10^0. What holds is L(B)=L(-B)^T, not L=L^T. Switching the field off returns |L_12-L_21| to the 10^-15 level, so the shape of the condition changes only when a field is present. The requirement is time reversal, which also reverses the field, so the fine-grained property of Paper 77 appears here as a condition. The separator is how many states are needed──the first three are statements about one operator, while the fourth needs B and -B side by side. Under Paper 300, the first three carry only an operator and the fourth also carries the sign of an external field, so they split three against one. The difference shows in practice: a non-reciprocal device needs something that breaks time reversal, and breaking symmetry alone will not do. Paper 143 found minimum entropy production to be a theorem with a fence, and the Onsager relation is one plank of it, itself changing shape under a field. So carrying the explanation of the first three across to the fourth produces an error. To be honest──the Onsager relations were not proved; the derivation from microscopic reversibility was not entered and only the shape of the relation was examined. The matrices are illustrative and belong to no substance. Only linear response was treated, nonlinear cases were not, and no isolator or circulator was designed. It is not claimed that four exhausts the list, nor that the four are the same theorem, nor that they are unrelated. What can be said is that they share a shape while requiring different things, and no further. On the making of this work: The ideas and content of this work stem from the author's own considerations. Assistance from an AI (a large language model) was used for structuring, English translation, and checking the algebra. Any remaining errors or misinterpretations are solely the author's. Feedback and corrections are sincerely appreciated. Keywords: reciprocity theorem, Onsager reciprocal relations, Helmholtz reciprocity, Betti's theorem, time-reversal symmetry. ----- 本稿の射程(射程注記):新しい定理も法則も主張しない──ヘルムホルツ、ローレンツ、ベッティ、オンサーガーのいずれの相反関係も標準的である。オンサーガー関係を証明しない──微視的可逆性からの導出には立ち入らず、関係の形だけを数で見る。実在の材料を扱わない──行列は説明のために置いたもので、特定の物質の係数ではない。非線形な場合に広げない──線形応答の枠内だけを見る。相反でない素子の設計を述べない──アイソレータやサーキュレータの実装は主題ではない。四つで尽きるとは書かない──数えたのは四つで、他に無いとは主張しない。「同じ定理だ」とも「無関係だ」とも書かない──共有しているのは形であり、要求している条件が違う。既刊との関係:論文143 なのに、L(B) と L(-B) の転置は差 0.00x10^0 で一致する(第3節)。 第四に、磁場を切れば普通の対称性に戻る──B=0 では |L_12-L_21| が 10^-15 の桁に落ちる(第3節)。 第五に、条件の形が違う──前三つは一つの行列について言えるが、四つ目は二つの状態(B と -B)を並べないと書けない(第4節)。
