candidates.title: ẸSAN AND THE MORAL CONSEQUENCES OF ACTION IN YORÙBÁ THOUGHT: BEYOND THE LANGUAGE OF “KARMA”
candidates.abstract: The concept of ẹ̀san occupies an important place in discussions of Yorùbá ethics, reciprocity and moral consequence. In popular discourse, ẹ̀san is sometimes translated as “karma” or “retribution,” but such translations can obscure important distinctions within Yorùbá moral thought. This paper examines ẹ̀san as a concept of consequence within Yorùbá ethical and religious thought, drawing particularly on philosophical scholarship concerning Yorùbá morality, character, reciprocity and divine justice. It argues that ẹ̀san is better understood as a principle through which actions generate consequences than as a simple mechanism of revenge or punishment. Scholarly discussions indicate that the consequences associated with ẹ̀san may be positive or negative, depending on the moral quality of the action, and may extend beyond the immediate individual to family and community. The paper further examines the relationship between ẹ̀san, ìwà (character), Olódùmarè and moral responsibility. It cautions against equating ẹ̀san uncritically with the South Asian concept of karma or with Christian notions of eternal punishment. Rather than assuming that these concepts are interchangeable, the paper considers the distinctive conceptual vocabulary through which Yorùbá thought understands moral consequence, reciprocity and justice. It concludes that ẹ̀san provides a significant indigenous category for examining how ethical action is understood to produce consequences within Yorùbá moral experience.

candidates.title: Foundational Principles of Effective E-Mentoring
candidates.abstract: Abstract Effective e-mentoring requires intentional design grounded in relational principles that transcend technological tools. This chapter establishes four foundational principles: trust as the bedrock of mentoring relationships, reciprocity that honors mutual growth and learning, boundaries that protect both mentors and mentees from overextension while maintaining authentic connection, and developmental orientation that centers long-term growth over transactional problem-solving. These principles operate differently in digital environments where relational cues are limited and interactions feel more formal. The chapter explores how trust must be actively built through consistency and transparency, how reciprocity manifests in digital contexts, how boundaries require explicit negotiation around response times and availability, and how developmental mentoring resists quick-fix solutions in favor of sustained support. Rather than providing prescriptive templates, the chapter offers practitioners a conceptual framework for designing e-mentoring that remains human-centered, relationally grounded, and developmentally sound regardless of platform or modality.

candidates.title: Q-learning dynamics of trust games on temporal higher-order networks
candidates.venue: Physica A Statistical Mechanics and its Applications
candidates.abstract: Trust is the fundamental cornerstone of social interactions. Traditional networked trust games are limited to static pairwise topologies, failing to capture multi-body and temporal dynamic interactions in real systems, while also relying on immediate payoffs without reinforcement learning optimization and lacking validation on real datasets. To address these issues, we construct a Q-learning-driven multi-player trust game model on temporal higher-order networks using the SocioPatterns datasets (conference, hospital, office) and a hierarchical time aggregation method. Simulation results suggest that high learning rate and discount factor tend to facilitate the emergence of network trust behavior under the investigated parameter configurations. Besides, temporal higher-order topology exerts a positive effect in alleviating the adverse impact of social dilemmas for the conference and hospital datasets under larger time-window aggregation. This work reveals the coupling mechanism between temporal higher-order structures and the Q-learning update rule, providing a new perspective on understanding the evolution of trust behavior in real-world complex dynamic higher-order social environments.

candidates.title: It’s more fun together: building networks for impact
candidates.venue: UNSWorks (University of New South Wales, Sydney, Australia)
candidates.abstract: This Professional Development Workshop reimagines networking and collaboration in academia as acts of psychological safety, reciprocity, and joy. Drawing on Edmondson’s (2019) psychological safety, Wenger’s (1998) communities of practice, and Bourdieu’s (1986) social capital, the session equips participants to transform networking from performance into authentic connection. Through experiential, reflective activities, participants map networks, craft purposeful ‘asks’, and build trust-based collaborations. The workshop debunks myths of extroversion and performance, promoting curiosity, generosity, and play as drivers of academic engagement. Attendees leave with a personalised activation plan to cultivate sustainable, interdisciplinary, and joyful professional relationships that strengthen higher education communities.

candidates.title: Child and Parental Contributions to Parent–Child Interaction in Autism
candidates.abstract: This study examines child and parental factors associated with observed parent–child interaction in families of preschool autistic children. Using data from approximately 70 children and their participating parents, the study investigates whether child social-adaptive functioning, behavioral and emotion-regulation difficulties, parental reflective functioning, and parental self-compassion make distinct contributions to the quality of parent–child interaction. Parent–child interactions are assessed using the Coding Interactive Behavior (CIB) system, focusing on dyadic reciprocity, parental sensitivity, child involvement, dyadic negative states, and parental intrusiveness. The study also examines whether parental self-compassion buffers associations between child dysregulation and interaction difficulties. Mixed-effects models will account for the nesting of parent–child observations within children.

candidates.title: Language, Culture, and Ethics: Discourse Strategies from The Global South for Shaping Global Business Norms
candidates.venue: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ENGLISH LANGUAGE AND COMMUNICATION STUDIES
candidates.pdf_url: https://iiardjournals.org/get/IJELCS/VOL. 11 NO. 6 2026/Language, Culture, and Ethics Discourse 61-66.pdf
candidates.abstract: Language is more than a tool of communication; it is a carrier of culture, values, and ethical worldviews. In the Global South, discourse strategies embedded in local languages and cultural practices provide unique insights into how business ethics can be reframed for global relevance. This paper explores how linguistic choices, such as metaphors of community, narratives of reciprocity, and culturally grounded expressions of responsibility, shape ethical expectations in business interactions. Drawing on examples from African, Asian, and Latin American contexts, the study demonstrates how local discourse practices challenge dominant Western paradigms of individualism and profit maximization, instead foregrounding collective accountability, relational trust, and sustainability. By analyzing these discourse strategies, the paper argues that the Global South contributes not only alternative ethical frameworks but also communicative models that can reshape global business norms. The research calls for a decolonized approach to business ethics that recognizes the power of language and culture in shaping moral economies, and positions the Global South as a vital source of ethical innovation with global impact.

candidates.title: A vida como jogo: regras espirituais, liberdade humana e responsabilidade na construção de uma existência com sentido
candidates.abstract: This article analyzes the metaphor of life as a game and argues that living consciously requires understanding the ethical, spiritual, and existential rules that guide human choices. The reflection builds upon Florence Scovel Shinn, for whom life is a game whose dynamics involve the spoken word, faith, expectation, love, and action, and engages in a dialogue with game theory in Johan Huizinga and Bernard Suits, the pursuit of meaning in Viktor Frankl, human agency in Albert Bandura, and Kenneth Pargament’s studies on spirituality and coping. A qualitative, conceptual, and hermeneutic approach is adopted, based on a critical and integrative review of the literature. It is argued that the game metaphor is fruitful when it acknowledges five elements: the existence of rules, situated freedom, purpose, consequences, and the possibility of learning. However, it becomes morally dangerous when it reduces suffering, poverty, illness, or injustice to an alleged individual inability to "play well." It concludes that spiritual rules should not be understood as magical formulas to control events, but as principles of discernment and conduct that allow one to respond to circumstances with truth, responsibility, hope, discipline, reciprocity, and meaning. Winning the game of life is not about mastering all conditions, but about remaining whole, learning, serving, and responsibly transforming attainable reality.

candidates.title: Strategic Asymmetry: Rethinking China’s Diplomatic Paradigm Toward the Global South
candidates.abstract: China’s diplomacy toward the Global South is becoming increasingly embedded in multilateral mechanisms and normative frameworks. The country’s dual identity as both an emerging great power and self-identified member of the Global South has given rise to a distinctive mode of South–South cooperation that eludes conventional theoretical explanations. While the “win–win” paradigm remains a normative staple of discourse on international cooperation, it encounters structural constraints in practice that include divergent interests, institutional and resource asymmetries, and temporal misalignments in reciprocity. This paper addresses the central research question of how to account theoretically for China’s growing tendency toward a paradigm of a single winner in the form of unilateral concessions and a strategic tolerance for asymmetry within cooperation efforts. By adopting an integrated theoretical framework, this paper argues that the initial single-winner paradigm does not represent a negation of win–win but rather its enabling condition under asymmetric structures. It represents a strategy that is temporally embedded and norm-generating while prioritizing delayed returns, reputational capital, and moral legitimacy. By reframing mutual gains beyond static symmetry, the single-winner paradigm offers an alternative logic for understanding China’s value-based diplomacy and its implications for the global order.

candidates.title: Supervisory Support and Retail Employees' Intention to Stay: A Context-Sensitive Conceptual Model of Organisational Commitment
candidates.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
candidates.abstract: ABSTRACTEmployee retention remains a strategic challenge in retail because frontline employeessustain service delivery under demanding and economically constrained conditions. Thisconceptual article develops a context-sensitive explanation of how supervisory supportmay influence employees’ intention to stay through organisational commitment. Anintegrative, theory-driven literature review was used to synthesise scholarship onsupervisory support, organisational commitment, intention to stay, and retention, withparticular attention to retail and service settings and South African evidence. SocialExchange Theory provides the overarching logic of reciprocity; Leader–Member Exchangeexplains the quality of supervisor–employee relationships; and Organisational SupportTheory explains how supervisory behaviour can be interpreted as an organisational signal.The proposed framework treats affective, normative and continuance commitment asdistinct mediating pathways and positions job security, compensation, career opportunities,organisational fairness, labour-market alternatives and quality of work-life as contextualconditions that may alter these relationships. Seven propositions are advanced for empiricaltesting. The article contributes by integrating relational, psychological and structuralexplanations into a parsimonious model that asks not only whether employees stay, butwhy they stay and under what conditions retention is sustainable.Keywords: supervisory support; organisational commitment; intention to stay; employeeretention; retail sector; organisational support

candidates.title: CROSS-BORDER ECONOMIC RELATIONS OF THE KHMER COMMUNITY IN TAY NINH PROVINCE FROM AN ECONOMIC ANTHROPOLOGY PERSPECTIVE
candidates.venue: Tạp chí Khoa học xã hội Thành phố Hồ Chí Minh
candidates.abstract: Cross-border economic relations are among the defining characteristics of ethnic communities living along the Vietnam-Cambodia border. Among the Khmer community in Tay Ninh Province, cross-border activities not only serve as important livelihood strategies but are also deeply embedded in kinship ties, community networks, and cultural norms that have evolved over generations. Drawing on primary data collected from a survey of 100 households, five in-depth interviews, and one focus group discussion conducted in Tay Ninh Province, this study applies Karl Polanyi’s economic anthropology framework to examine the nature of cross-border economic relations. The findings reveal that the economic activities of the border Khmer are not governed solely by the market principle of profit maximisation. Rather, they are shaped by the three fundamental principles of economic integration identified by Polanyi: reciprocity, redistribution, and market exchange. Among these, kinship relations, social networks, and community trust constitute the social foundations that sustain cross-border economic practices, even amid deepening economic integration and increasingly stringent border governance. The study therefore demonstrates the explanatory value of Polanyi’s economic anthropology in understanding the social embeddedness of cross-border economic activities among ethnic minority communities in contemporary Vietnam.

candidates.title: Membership and Fraternal Ontologies
candidates.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
candidates.abstract: First release of two layered OWL 2 DL + SKOS ontologies for describing membership organisations as Linked Open Data. Membership Organisations (https://w3id.org/membership, prefixes mbr: and mbrc:): membership organisations of every kind, closed or open: clubs, societies, student nations, associations, political parties and trade unions. Membership lifecycle, admission and fees, offices and terms, gatherings, distinctions and conferrals, premises, reciprocity, catalogue facts. Fraternal Orders and Sororities (https://w3id.org/fraternal, prefixes fraternal: and fraternalc:): extends the membership ontology with degree systems, initiation, lodges and grand bodies, insignia, recognition and amity, and orders of chivalry with legitimacy recorded as dated assessments. Also included: SKOS codelists, SHACL shapes, SSSOM mappings to Wikidata and Getty AAT, fictional test data and competency questions. candidates.title: Proportionality, Equality, and Judicial Integrity: Reinterpreting Lex Talionis in Pentateuchal Narratives
candidates.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
candidates.abstract: The principle of lex talionis, often summed up as “eye for an eye” and “tooth for a tooth,” has been widely seen as a biblical endorsement of retaliation. However, this study re-examines the principle within its legal context in the Pentateuch, focusing on Exodus 21:23-25, Leviticus 24:17-22, and Deuteronomy 19:16-21. Employing a comparative exegetical approach, the paper examined the literary, legal, lexical, and theological aspects of these texts to ascertain how lex talionis functions in various legal frameworks. Findings revealed that this principle does not operate as absolute authorisation for personal vengeance. Rather, Exodus 21:23-25 governs bodily retaliation through proportionality; Leviticus 24:17-22 places reciprocal justice within the realm of community equality, fairness, and a shared legal standard; and Deuteronomy 19:16-21 applies this idea of correspondence to malicious testimony, protecting judicial integrity and ensuring accountability. The paper concluded that these differences mark a significant evolution in Pentateuchal law, where the concept of reciprocity is increasingly shaped by proportionality, equality, institutional authority, due process, and deterrence. Lex talionis therefore emerges not just as a principle of retaliation but as an instrument of regulated justice aimed at curbing excess, protecting individuals, maintaining community order, and upholding the integrity of legal institutions.

candidates.title: Navigating rénqíng and face: A four-phase sequential model of money-borrowing requests in rural China
candidates.abstract: Abstract In rural China, money-borrowing is not merely a financial transaction but a complex social practice. This study explores the pragmatic strategies of money-borrowing requests through qualitative interviews with 29 rural residents. The analysis identifies a four-phase sequential model that maps the communicative architecture of these requests, comprising (1) a preparatory and framing phase; (2) a core request phase; (3) a support phase involving facework, justification, and reciprocity; and (4) a potential intensification and coercion phase. Furthermore, the analysis shows how recurrent strategy patterns reveal the cultural script for negotiating trust, face, and rénqíng (人情). Four core components of this script are identified: the primacy of relational framing through fictive kinship; the function of justification and hearer consideration as prerequisites; the verbal construction of trust through promises; and a structural preference for indirectness as a risk management strategy. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that money-borrowing in rural China is not a simple economic transaction but a socially embedded practice, systematically shaped by the cultural logic of rénqíng and face. More broadly, the study argues that high-stakes requests should be analyzed not merely as inventories of individual strategies, but as sequentially organized, culturally saturated communicative events through which social obligations, interpersonal trust, and face dynamics are pragmatically constituted.

candidates.title: Unheard horizons
candidates.abstract: This chapter reinterprets principal burnout not as a failure of resilience, but as a breakdown of understanding within the relational and ethical work of educational leadership. While acknowledging that burnout arises from multiple, intersecting pressures, the chapter focuses on parent engagement as a significant site in which interpretive strain, emotional labour, and moral dissonance are intensified. Drawing on Gadamer&s;s philosophical hermeneutics, it examines how neoliberal schooling, shaped by market choice, performative accountability, and heightened parental scrutiny, has recast engagement as a space of contested meaning rather than reciprocal understanding. Through Gadamer&s;s notion of the fusion of horizons, burnout is understood as the cumulative effect of sustained interpretive asymmetry. School leaders are repeatedly required to understand parents, systems, and policy demands, while rarely being understood in return. Over time, this erosion of reciprocity destabilises trust, deepens emotional labour, and weakens the ethical coherence on which humane leadership depends. By foregrounding leaders&s; interpretive struggles, the chapter reframes wellbeing as a dialogic condition grounded in recognition, openness, and shared meaning rather than individual self-management. In doing so, it challenges the assumption that parent engagement is inherently positive and invites a critical reorientation toward partnerships capable of sustaining difference, mutual understanding, and the interpretive conditions of educational leadership.

candidates.title: Legal and Ethical Dimensions of Organ and Tissue Transplantation: A Review with a Focus on Türkiye
candidates.venue: Journal of Bursa Faculty of Medicine
candidates.abstract: Organ and tissue transplantation is an essential medical intervention that improves survival and quality of life in patients with end-stage organ failure; however, it also raises complex legal and ethical issues concerning bodily autonomy, consent, determination of death, organ allocation, and commercial exploitation. This review aims to evaluate the main legal regulations and ethical issues related to organ and tissue transplantation and to examine the areas of convergence and conflict between law and ethics. In this context, international biomedical regulations and Turkish law are discussed with particular emphasis on valid consent and informed consent, protection of living and deceased donors, brain death, individual autonomy and the role of the family in deceased donation, justice in organ allocation, religious and sociocultural factors, and organ trafficking. The 2025 legal amendment in Türkiye, which gives priority to the donor’s previously expressed will over contrary views of relatives, has strengthened the legal protection of individual autonomy. However, granting allocation priority to the spouses and first-degree relatives of donors has introduced a new ethical debate concerning reciprocity, justice, and equality. In conclusion, although legal regulations and fundamental ethical principles largely converge in organ and tissue transplantation, dynamic issues such as organ scarcity, justice in allocation, public trust, and socioeconomic vulnerability require continuous legal and ethical evaluation.

candidates.title: Constructing relational resilience: Governance, power and the limits of transformation in Aotearoa New Zealand’s hill country farming
candidates.abstract: This study investigates how resilience is relationally constructed within Aotearoa New Zealand’s hill country farming systems. Drawing on qualitative interviews with hill-country farmers, and applying a social relational resilience perspective together with the Resilience Capacities Framework, the research examines how capacities for persistence, adaptation, and transformation emerge through relationships among farmers, communities, markets, and governance institutions. The findings show that persistence is sustained through long-term trust, reciprocity, stewardship, and intergenerational social ties, while adaptive capacity depends on diverse social networks, collective learning, and the integration of heterogeneous knowledges. However, adaptive opportunities remain uneven and are shaped by unequal access to networks, markets, and institutional support. Transformative capacity was comparatively weak across cases, constrained by fragmented governance relationships, limited institutional trust, and power asymmetries that restricted collaborative problem-solving and cross-scale engagement. The study argues that resilience is not an attribute of individual farmers nor reducible to capital stocks, but an emergent and relational process shaped by everyday interactions, governance dynamics, and socio-political context. By operationalising the Resilience Capacities Framework empirically, the paper contributes to relational resilience scholarship and demonstrates the importance of relational infrastructures, inclusive governance, and co-produced adaptation pathways for rural sustainability transformations.

candidates.title: Doing fair pay. Implications from the Austrian experience
candidates.venue: European Journal of Cultural Management and Policy
candidates.abstract: Since 2020, Austria has introduced measures for fair pay in the independent arts and culture sector as part of a broader fairness reform. Drawing on policy documents and monitoring reports, this policy brief analyses the first years of the framework’s implementation. The learnings show that the Fair Pay initiative demonstrates a strong commitment to closing remuneration gaps, while a structural transformation of longstanding precarious working conditions requires a broader systemic approach. The Austrian case reveals that sustainable reform of working conditions in the independent non-profit arts and culture sector hinges not only on fiscal commitment but also on governance coordination, interest-group representation, adequate statistical visibility, cross-domain cultural awareness, and supportive transnational regulation. These insights contribute to the growing movement across Europe that aims to strengthen cultural policy commitment, the status of artists and professionals, and the principles of public goods.

candidates.title: Fribourg Ultimatum Game in Schizophrenia Study
candidates.abstract: This dataset contains 128-channel EEG recorded during an Ultimatum Game (UG) task in patients with psychosis episodes (n=19) and healthy controls (n=24). Participants played the game in both the responder and proposer roles. Data were collected at the University of Fribourg, Switzerland, to study social decision-making in schizophrenia.

candidates.title: Biases in individual and social decision-making
candidates.abstract: Human behavior is shaped by the interplay between innate response tendencies and experience–dependent learning. Automatic Pavlovian reactions, i.e. approach to potential rewards and inhibition in the face of potential punishments, often facilitate rapid, adaptive action, yet they can conflict with instrumental demands that require acting (or withholding action) contrary to these biases. This thesis investigates how such biases shape learning and decision–making and how social contexts modulate their expression. A central theme is that overcoming Pavlovian–instrumental conflict carries measurable mental effort, and that social evaluation selectively perturbs the mechanisms supporting action generation and reward processing. I take a behavioral, physiological and computational approach to (i) formalize Pavlovian–instrumental interactions in reinforcement learning, (ii) quantify the mental effort involved in decision–making under incongruency using pupillometry and (iii) dissociate the effects of mere social presence and social evaluation on learning. First, I synthesize prior theoretical and empirical work to motivate a reinforcement learning framework in which Pavlovian value signals invigorate or suppress action independently of instrumental contingencies, while frontal control processes can down–regulate these influences when they are maladaptive. Within this framework, I derive testable predictions linking latent variables (action values, prediction errors, and Pavlovian conflict) to both behavior choices, reaction times) and trial–by–trial task–evoked pupillary responses as a proxy for arousal/effort. I then test these predictions in a Go/NoGo learning paradigm that orthogonalizes action requirements (Go vs. NoGo) and outcome valence (reward vs. punishment). Across seven candidate reinforcement learning models, variants that include a Pavlovian component (reward→invigoration, punishment→inhibition) best explain human behavior, and the simplest of these, with a single outcome sensitivity and a learned Pavlovian value, wins; model and parameter recovery confirm that this conclusion is identifiable. Behaviorally, participants are more accurate under congruent mappings (rewarded actions and preventive inactions) than under incongruent ones (omission schedule and active avoidance), with the omission schedule particularly impaired, and respond faster for reward than for punishment. Physiologically, the task-evoked pupil response differentiates trial types by Pavlovian–instrumental congruence at the cue, by the executed action at the decision, and by losses and omitted rewards at the outcome. Time–resolved model–based analyses ground these effects in the latent variables of the winning model: the learned Pavlovian value scales the pupil during cue evaluation and drives dilation at the decision when it opposes the required action, while an unsigned Pavlovian prediction error, i.e. surprise irrespective of its sign, governs the outcome–locked response. At every stage the pupil tracks the Pavlovian rather than the instrumental quantity, linking latent learning signals to physiological effort. To assess social modulation, I repeat the task within subjects across three contexts: individual performance, passive social presence and active social evaluation with contingent payoffs. Social evaluation produces a selective deficit in action learning: participants show impaired acquisition and execution of Go responses while NoGo learning remains intact. Concomitantly, phasic pupillary responses associated with action requirements are attenuated under evaluation, consistent with a reduction in available cognitive resources or altered noradrenergic arousal when decisions are made under social judgment. Despite stable average Pavlovian and Go biases across contexts, evaluation shifts Positivity bias (reward vs. avoidance performance) toward negative values, indicating a conservative reweighting of reward processing in evaluative settings. Together, these findings provide a unified account of how Pavlovian biases shape human learning and choice, how cognitive control overcomes these biases at measurable physiological cost, and how social evaluation selectively disrupts action generation and reward processing. The work clarifies the computational roles of Pavlovian and instrumental systems, grounds the pupil response in model–derived variables resolved across the course of a decision, and isolates social evaluation, distinct from mere presence, as a driver of action–specific learning impairments. Limitations include the interpretive specificity of pupillometry and the need to generalize beyond the Go/NoGo domain; I outline multi–method extensions (EEG/fMRI/pharmacology) and broader decision paradigms (risk, delay, effort). Overall, the thesis advances a testable framework for understanding when and why humans fail to act optimally, even when they “know better”, and how social environments can tip the balance between reflexive and goal–directed control.

candidates.title: Theory of Scene: Breaking the Symmetry Trap in Multi-Agent LLM Coordination
candidates.abstract: Multi-agent systems built on large language models (LLMs) are largely homogeneous, as their agents behave alike even across distinct LLMs. We show that when such agents act concurrently without communication, they collide on targets they must split and diverge on targets they must take together, a double failure we term the symmetry trap. Theory of Mind (ToM), widely used for coordination without communication, cannot escape this trap, since homogeneous agents form the same prediction of one another and respond to it in the same way. We propose Theory of Scene (ToS), a training-free reasoning schema in which each agent reads its public role, the only difference between the agents, and the task context they all observe. Homogeneous agents thereby derive one division of labor, each taking the part its role fixes, which turns homogeneity from the cause of the trap into the cure. ToS reads the role together with the scene through role gating, which determines whether ownership overlaps or is already divided, and the task context through task coupling, which infers whether the team must converge on each target, divide it, or take its stages in turn. We evaluate on DivvyBench, a controlled environment we introduce, whose target types make an episode Competitive, Cooperative, or Mixed across Tabletop, Airspace, and Household scenarios, and on two established agentic benchmarks, GovSim and Overcooked. ToS outperforms all six baselines on every benchmark, and each baseline falls far behind it in at least one setting. Against ToM given the same inputs, ToS raises the DivvyBench success rate from 71.1% to 99.6%, the GovSim total gain from 207 to 400, and the Overcooked level-normalized throughput from 1.41 to 1.67.

candidates.title: When and Why are Social Categories Overused Relative to Individuating Information? A Bayesian Approach to Identifying Biases in Impression Formation Processes
candidates.abstract: When making inferences about others, people often need to integrate multiple types of information, including the person’s social categories (e.g., occupation) as well as other “individuating” information (e.g., their behaviors). The current work re-examines this integration process, to understand when and why it produces biases involving over-reliance on category information. We identify two key challenges in identifying such biases, and develop a novel Bayesian modelling approach to overcome them. As a first step in applying this approach, the current work examined a set of novel predictions based on viewing the Continuum Model of impression formation in light of this Bayesian approach. Specifically, a series of six studies tested whether occupation categories might be overused in general, or especially in conditions thought to reduce effortful processing (i.e., greater cognitive load or information consistency). Results showed no evidence of category overuse, nor of shifts in this direction, in any of these conditions (though some ambiguity remained about the load manipulation’s effectiveness). This provides initial evidence against the idea that intrinsic differences in how these categories are processed or represented will lead to their overuse. A seventh study provided the first direct evidence of a case where categories were overused: when contextual factors (i.e., background goals) made them the category especially relevant, while processing resources were limited. More broadly, the current work developed the theoretical and methodological foundations for identifying category overuse that stems from biased inference processes, and demonstrated the power of this approach for understanding when and why such biases occur.

candidates.title: Dimensional and Categorical Predictors of Theory of Mind Network Activation: A transdiagnostic fMRI Study in Psychiatric Inpatients
candidates.abstract: Socio-cognitive alterations are widely observed across different psychiatric conditions, yet it remains unclear whether these deficits map onto distinct diagnostic categories or represent a shared transdiagnostic phenotype, driven by dimensional psychopathological symptom severity.This study evaluates Theory of Mind (ToM) network activation during a naturalistic functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) movie paradigm in 313 participants, including 91 healthy controls and 222 psychiatric inpatients across five distinct diagnostic clusters (substance use, schizophrenia spectrum, affective, anxiety, and personality disorders). Frequentist analyses revealed decreased ToM-selective activity in psychiatric patients, compared to controls across all ToM regions of interest (ROIs). No significant difference emerged between diagnostic groups, but ROI activation correlated negatively with Adult Self-Report (ASR) scales (  Total Problems, Internalising, Externalising ). Subsequent Bayesian analysis of covariance (ANCOVAs) consistently favoured models that excluded traditional categorical diagnoses, suggesting that dimensional measures, especially Total Problems and Internalising, provided substantially greater predictive utility for ToM-related regional brain activation. Our findings challenge traditional categorical classifications in neurobiological research as they suggest that atypical mentalising might reflect a shared transdiagnostic vulnerability.  Highlights  Reduced Theory of Mind specific activation in psychiatric inpatients presents as a shared, transdiagnostic feature. Theory of Mind specific activation shows no disorder-specific patterns across five distinct clinical diagnostic clusters. Bayesian analyses consistently favour continuous psychopathology dimensions over categorical classifications in predicting Theory of Mind specific activation

candidates.title: Cerebellar anodal transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) improves implicit mentalizing sequence learning: A double-blind sham-controlled study
candidates.abstract: An increasing number of studies have revealed that the posterior cerebellum plays a vital role in mentalizing by identifying and learning social action sequences that render social interaction more fluent, coordinated, and predictable. An implicit social sequencing task, the Belief serial response time (SRT) task, was administered during and 30 min after targeting the cerebellum with anodal transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS; 2 mA for 20 min, electrode 2 cm below the inion). In a previous study, this setup did not show significant improvement in response times. We reasoned that the familiar and overlearned nature of attributing social beliefs resulted in a ceiling effect and thus left very little margin for improvement on the task. The current study developed a more difficult version of the Belief SRT task. Using a double-blind sham-controlled protocol, 60 participants received either anodal tDCS or sham tDCS using the same stimulation protocol. Results showed that participants receiving anodal tDCS responded faster when the sequence of actions was repeated as opposed to totally randomized compared with participants who received sham tDCS. These findings suggest a positive effect of anodal cerebellar tDCS on implicit mentalizing sequence learning, supporting a causal role of the cerebellum in this learning process. This holds promise for treating clinical populations with limited social and sequencing capacities (e.g., autism) with anodal tDCS.

candidates.title: Self-Referential Social Processing in Schizophrenia and Bipolar Disorder: Advancing Theoretical Precision and Clinical Insights with Model-Based Neuroscience
candidates.abstract: Background. Individuals with schizophrenia (SZ) and bipolar disorder (BD) often misjudge whether social cues, like eye contact, are meant for them, which can fuel symptoms and functional impairment. These difficulties appear to stem from disruptions in how social information is dynamically processed (“evidence accumulation”). We used neurocognitive joint modeling to investigate which neural signals shape evidence accumulation during gaze perception and whether these brain-behavior links help explain disrupted self-referential social processing.Methods. Leveraging EEG data from N=99 SZ, BD, and healthy controls (HC) during a self-referential gaze perception task, we built joint drift-diffusion models characterizing how different trial-level EEG features translated to evidence accumulation and behavior. Joint models were compared against each other (and models using task-averaged EEG or behavior only) for their ability to predict task behavior and relevant clinical dimensions, including paranoia, functioning, and cognition. We examined whether the best-performing model differentiated patients and HC.Results. The best-performing joint model explained evidence accumulation through trial-level fluctuations—not task averages—in two neural signals: CPP and frontal midline theta, implicated in subjective deliberation/certainty and top-down modulation, respectively. Less reliable translation of trial-level CPP signals to evidence accumulation impaired gaze perception in SZ and BD. Mapping how trial-level theta dynamics translated to evidence accumulation captured paranoia and functioning better than behavior or task-averaged neural metrics alone.Conclusions. Model-based approaches that embrace the within-person variability of neural signals may reveal more nuanced, clinically relevant perspectives on the pathophysiology of SZ and BD than those using task-averaged brain activity or behavior alone.

candidates.title: Modeling decision dynamics disentangles working memory, cognitive control and reinforcement learning and reveals clinical differences
candidates.abstract: Various neurocognitive processes contribute to reinforcement learning (RL) and decision making, requiring careful task designs and computational modeling to disentangle them. People rely on capacity-limited working memory (WM) to rapidly and flexibly adapt behavior during learning, together with slower incremental RL processes that support robust long-term retention. The RLWM paradigm was developed to isolate these contributions by manipulating WM demands during learning. Empirical and computational advances support the separability of such processes, but only imperfectly, because a given choice can often equally be attributed to use of WM vs. RL. Here, we show that jointly modeling decision dynamics - accounting not only for choices but also response time distributions, together with hierarchical Bayesian parameter estimation - improves the ability to disentangle separable learning and cognitive control processes. Despite added complexity, models with decision dynamics improved parameter recovery and yielded accurate out-of-sample prediction for choices in a held-out test phase after learning. In contrast, models fit only to choices produced an inflation of RL learning rates and failed the out-of-sample test. Moreover, joint modeling also revealed a novel neurocognitive process by which participants proactively widen decision boundaries to increase response caution under increased WM load. Applying our model to patients with schizophrenia revealed a deficit in proactive control mechanisms as well as slowed incremental RL, which were masked by previous choice-only models, while replicating previously established WM deficits. In summary, we show how joint modeling enables accurate, model-based and mechanism-oriented computational phenotyping of psychopathologies.

candidates.title: An LLM canary in the online data coalmine: Bayesian reasoning problems as a capability-gap test for LLM contamination in online samples
candidates.abstract: The growing use of large language models (LLMs) by participants in online studies threatens the validity of behavioral research data. I propose that Bayesian reasoning problems, which have decades of well-replicated human performance benchmarks, can serve as calibrated detectors of LLM contamination in online samples - an approach I call a capability-gap test. In two preregistered pilots of a Bayesian reasoning training tool (N = 148), participants' accuracy on positive predictive value (PPV) calculation problems reached roughly three times established human performance ceilings. Specifically, 57% of Pilot 2 participants achieved perfect 5/5 scores, against a meta-analytic ceiling of approximately 24% for a single problem presented in natural frequency format, a level at which perfect scores are effectively unattainable. Including two outcome measures - accuracy (correct numerical answer) and Bayesian algorithm use (evidence of the reasoning process) - allows researchers to distinguish LLM contamination from authentic learning effects: accuracy detects contamination, while algorithm use preserves treatment effect signals. This is itself a signal detection problem, structurally analogous to the mass screenings for low-prevalence problems around which the Bayesian reasoning literature was developed. Bayesian reasoning problems offer four advantages as contamination detectors: well-established human performance ceilings from meta-analyses, a large human-LLM performance gap, known reference distributions enabling nuanced assessment, and ease of embedding in existing surveys. I provide practical recommendations for using these problems as data quality diagnostics in online research.

candidates.title: The Evolution of Financial Time Series Forecasting: From Classical Econometrics to Temporal Foundation Models and Multimodal LLMs
candidates.abstract: Financial time series forecasting sits at the intersection of applied mathematics, econometrics, and machine learning. The data generating processes involved are characterized by non-stationarity, regime-dependent volatility clustering, very low signal-to-noise ratios, and reflexive feedback between market participants and asset prices. Over roughly six decades, the dominant methodology has moved through five recognizable phases: classical linear econometrics (ARMA, ARIMA, regularized VAR, VECM), conditional volatility modeling (ARCH/GARCH families, Stochastic Volatility), recursive online signal processing (LMS, RLS, Kalman filters), deep sequence learning (LSTMs, TCNs, patch-based Transformers, State Space Models), and the contemporary period (2024--2026) of Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs), Temporal Language Models (TLMs), and LLMs adapted for financial reasoning. For the purposes of the comparative analysis in Section~10, the deep learning phase is split into two paradigms (recurrent/convolutional networks and Transformer-based architectures), and the foundation model phase is similarly split into numerical TSFMs and multimodal LLM adapters, yielding seven paradigm entries in total. This paper traces that trajectory through the lens of what we call the Capacity-Adaptability Trilemma, a three-way tension between representational capacity, online adaptability, and structural interpretability. We also examine where foundation models fall short in financial contexts, documenting how benchmark contamination and architectural mismatches can cause large zero-shot models to underperform simple statistical baselines. To address this, we propose Econometrically-Informed Neural Networks (EINNs) as a way to embed econometric constraints into modern deep architectures. We present four self-contained synthetic experiments conducted on a MacBook Air M1. These provide limited empirical illustration of several paper claims: that model class rankings shift with SNR and nonlinearity structure (consistent with the trilemma framing), that a noise-dependent crossover exists between DLinear and PatchTST, that trained autoregressors do not beat naive persistence on synthetic random walks, and that the proposed VECM regularizer improves spread stationarity in a bivariate cointegrated setup.

candidates.title: Idiographic Memory Modelling in ACT-R Using Alternating Maximum Likelihood Estimation
candidates.abstract: Abstract Performance on memory tasks varies systematically between individuals and within individuals over time. However, computational models of memory are often fitted at the group level or summarise performance in a single parameter, potentially obscuring the distinct cognitive processes that give rise to this variation. Here we present a likelihood-based procedure for fitting the multi-parameter ACT-R declarative memory model at the level of the individual. Using this method, we jointly estimate five participant-level or idiographic parameters, each capturing a distinct component of memory performance, together with item-level variation in memorability. A parameter recovery study on synthetic data shows that these participant- and item-level parameters are jointly identifiable from realistic amounts of data on a typical spaced repetition memory task, requiring only about 40–90 observations of response accuracy and speed per participant. We demonstrate the method on a dataset of individuals with mild cognitive impairment and age-matched healthy controls, finding that mild cognitive impairment is marked by differences in three parameters signifying accelerated forgetting, less efficient memory retrieval, and general psychomotor slowing. These results show that the method can successfully decompose observed performance on a memory task into separable, individually interpretable components. More broadly, this work contributes to the development of fine-grained idiographic memory models that can capture dynamics in memory performance both between and within individuals, with applications in experimental research and applied settings, such as computational phenotyping for clinical diagnosis.

candidates.title: Transformer-Based Trust Estimation for Peer Learning in Reinforcement Learning
BMA: Backchain Memory Attacks Create Unauthorized Control Paths in LLM Agents
candidates.abstract: Persistent memory enables LLM agents to reuse prior experience, but creates a new security boundary: what an agent may remember is not what it should act on. We expose an unauthorized control path where edited low-trust evidence is consolidated into persistent memory, retrieved on a clean task, and used to drive a protected action. Crucially, the adversary neither writes memory nor alters the task. We introduce Backchain Memory Attack (BMA), a grey-box, LLM-driven inverse-planning attack that reasons backward from the target action to the memory that would trigger it, then to the evidence edit that would form it. BMA has two phases: preparation uses resettable trials to localize the first failed link and build experience; execution uses the frozen experience to rank and commit candidate edits without feedback. We introduce the Pathway-Certified Attack Success Rate (Path-CASR) to separate memory-mediated from coincidental hits: registered memory must form, be retrieved, drive the target behavior, and pass matched-intervention checks. Across four substrates and three decision backbones, BMA achieves 18.8% Macro Path-CASR, compared with 13.4% for the strongest access-matched baseline. Of BMA's behavioral hits, 60.3% pass all registered pathway and intervention checks versus 36.7% for the baseline. Frozen BMA edits retain 78.0% of their certified effect on average across four held-out consolidation policies. Representative memory-side controls leave 11.0% Path-CASR, whereas provenance-bound authorization reduces it to 2.0% while preserving 92.1% legitimate-action success.

candidates.title: Trust your gut: the neuro-gastroenteric mechanics of prediction and expectation
candidates.abstract: Living organisms constantly make probabilistic predictions about what they expect to see in their external environment, and actively solicit information from the environment to inform their predictions. This process is foundational for many frameworks including Active Inference and Predictive Processing. It relies on organisms having prior expectations, entailed by an internal generative model of the environment. Posterior expectations are updated based on the selected data, driven by prediction error minimization. However, failures to contextualize the precision or confidence placed in predictions, can give rise to perceptual abnormalities that are at the basis of various psychiatric conditions. Different factors can influence this process. Notably, disruptions in the gut microbiome have been implicated in some psychotic disorders. Gut microbial dysregulation has also been associated with alterations in neurotransmitter synthesis, metabolism, and turnover, which may affect processes involved in the encoding of precision of prediction errors. On the basis of this gut-brain connection, this Hypothesis and Theory article hypothesizes that the gut microbiome plays a role as a modulator of predictive processing, influencing how predictions are formed and expectations updated. Specifically, this article explores the importance of “mental model" embodiment, and considers the role of hippocampal activity in predictive coding and its modulation by the gut microbiome. Finally, it offers a novel perspective on the use of cortico-hippocampal-gastroenteric frameworks for inferring personalized dietary interventions in nutritional psychiatry.

candidates.title: The transformative power of tales: fostering language, empathy, and decolonial praxis in education
candidates.abstract: Storytelling is more than just entertainment; it is a basic cognitive and social process that helps people create meaning and develop critical abilities. This study makes the case that narrative-based practices ought to be acknowledged as a fundamental pedagogical engine that is important for many aspects of human development, including cognitive, social-emotional, and sociopolitical domains. The paper first examines how the brain’s innate propensity for narrative promotes causality, critical thinking, and advanced language acquisition, making stories a powerful medium for literacy and self-expression. It draws on research from developmental psychology, literary theory, and educational practice. Second, it explores how narrative fosters empathy and social skills, showing how the mental modeling of characters’ experiences serves as a “moral laboratory” for the development of Theory of Mind (ToM). Importantly, the analysis includes a section that makes the case that storytelling is both an act of epistemic justice and a decolonial praxis. The Eurocentric canon and the “danger of a single story” are challenged when marginalized voices and local knowledge systems are prioritized. This makes narrative a potent tool for resistance, identity formation, and systemic change in educational settings. Finally, the paper discusses how the practical implementation of these theoretical insights can be applied practically using evidence-based models, such as the Storytelling/Story-Acting (STSA) practice, mental state-focused reading, and Digital Storytelling (DST). These tactics show how teachers can incorporate narrative to support students’ overall development and develop the intercultural competency required for a fair, post-colonial society. / Keywords: storytelling, decolonial pedagogy, epistemic justice, language acquisition, empathy, narrative cognition, educational practice, intercultural competence

candidates.title: Editorial: Learning for democracy
candidates.abstract: The collection begins by revisiting foundational democratic theories and applying them to modern educational contexts. Yi-Huang Shih provides inspiration by revisiting John Dewey's ideas, framing democracy not just as a form of government but as a mode of associated living and communicated experience. Building on the conceptual nature of engagement, Helmut Heid, Michael Jüttler, and Tobias Kärner provide a rigorous conceptual analysis of student participation in the classroom, questioning whether and how these micro-level interactions serve as a legitimate basis for broader democracy education.Several papers examine the specific factors that drive or hinder student participation within higher education. Yang Lin and colleagues investigate the personal and institutional determinants of civic engagement, highlighting that student involvement is a product of both individual motivation and the institutional environment. This is complemented by the work of Ali Assad Watfa and Driss Ait Ali, whose research demonstrates the mediating effect of university citizenship promotion in transforming national loyalty into active student political participation.A significant portion of the Research Topic addresses how education functions in societies facing social fragmentation or the aftermath of conflict. In the context of intergroup tension, Devora Hellerstein and Mahmood Sindiani present "the roaming course," a method for fostering intergroup relationships among Arab and Jewish students within physical education teacher education, illustrating the power of shared physical activity in building democratic empathy. On a systemic level, Mohamed Yusuf Adan utilizes a "4Rs framework analysis" to explore the role of peace education in promoting social justice and sustainable peace in post-conflict societies, providing a structural lens for democratic reconstruction.Modern democracy also faces threats from within the digital and cultural spheres. Lucia Picarella examines the intersections of the digital society, specifically how "cancel culture" and "fake news" distort contemporary public discourse, presenting challenges for educators trying to foster rational democratic debate. In Chile, Jesús Marolla-Gajardo highlights the risks to democracy by analyzing the beliefs of teachers regarding the transmission of hate speech within teacher education, emphasizing the urgent need for pedagogical interventions against intolerance.The Research Topic also provides deep dives into specific regional challenges. Two papers focus on Indonesia: Sarbaini Sarbaini discusses the challenges and opportunities of enhancing civic education for nationalism in Indonesian higher education, balancing national identity with democratic values. Meanwhile, Rahmat Muhammad and colleagues offer an original research case study on rational choice and political imaging during legislative elections in East Luwu, providing empirical evidence of how democratic processes play out in resource-rich mining areas.A core theme emerging from these diverse studies is the need for more effective social models to drive change. Titus Alexander proposes that we view institutions as social models and 'dynamic theories'. This hypothesis suggests that social and political sciences can increase their impact by moving beyond observation and analysis to using research to actively inform and improve practice. Each paper in this collection explores different models of learning for democracy, whether for student participation in the classroom, intervening against hate speech, bridging differences through physical education or any of the other topics. The hypothesis proposes that scholars should work with practitioners to develop the working model itself, not just the conceptual theories about it, because every working model embodies a great deal of knowledge embedded in its infrastructure, norms, protocols, power dynamics, and relationships, as well as the beliefs and other mental models used to guide it (see Fig. 1). It argues that this can be seen as the social science equivalent of theories in the natural sciences. This approach suggests that learning for democracy is not a one-time educational event but a continuous process of theory, practice, reflection, research and evaluation, to continuously improve the model. It also recognises the importance of institutional support.In conclusion, the papers in this Research Topic demonstrate that while democracy is under pressure, universities and educators are developing innovative methods-from intergroup "roaming courses" to the "4Rs framework"-to strengthen it. The common thread is that learning for democracy must be an active, institutional priority that connects classroom participation with civic responsibility. By adopting dynamic social theories, the academic community can better equip the next generation to navigate digital misinformation, overcome social conflict, and revitalize democratic norms worldwide.

candidates.title: Next-Generation Cybersecurity: Architectural Resilience, Threat Paradigms, and the Shift to Zero-Trust in Distributed Ecosystems
candidates.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
candidates.abstract: Next-Generation Cybersecurity: Architectural Resilience, Threat Paradigms, and the Shift to Zero-Trust in Distributed Ecosystems 1. Introduction: The Disappearing Walls of the Digital World For decades, cybersecurity operated on a simple mental model: the Castle-and-Moat. An organization built massive stone walls (firewalls) and dug deep moats around its physical office. Anyone outside was considered an enemy, and anyone inside was trusted by default. Once an employee crossed the drawbridge with an ID badge or a VPN password, they had broad access to wander the corridors of the castle—opening file cabinets, browsing internal servers, and viewing databases. This model worked well when every worker sat at a desk in the same building, using a desktop computer plugged into a company wall socket, accessing a server located in the basement. Today, that castle has dissolved: Distributed Ecosystems: Applications no longer run on single servers in the basement. They live spread across global cloud providers (Amazon, Google, Microsoft), edge devices, and remote home offices. Ephemeral Workloads: Many modern services run inside "containers"—tiny virtual programs that spin up in seconds to handle traffic and vanish minutes later. Hybrid Work: Employees access critical databases from home Wi-Fi networks, hotel lounges, and mobile phones across multiple time zones. Because there is no longer a physical perimeter to defend, treating the "inside" of a network as safe has become one of the most dangerous assumptions in computing. Next-generation cybersecurity replaces this outdated perimeter with two foundational principles: Zero-Trust Architecture (ZTA) and Architectural Resilience. 2. Modern Threat Paradigms: How Attackers Actually Operate To understand why security models had to change, we must look at how modern cyberattacks work. Attackers rarely smash directly through the front gates anymore; they use subtle, compound techniques designed to exploit implicit trust. A. Lateral Movement (The Hotel Keycard Problem) In an old network, once an attacker cracked a single, low-priority device—like a smart thermostat or an intern’s laptop—they were "inside." From there, they could quietly move sideways across the network (lateral movement), hopping from computer to computer until they found high-value assets like customer databases or payroll systems. It is the equivalent of a hotel where your room keycard can open every other bedroom door, the manager's office, and the bank vault downstairs. B. Supply-Chain Poisoning Modern software is rarely written entirely from scratch. Developers build applications by assembling hundreds of pre-existing open-source building blocks (libraries and packages). Attackers now target these third-party ingredients rather than the company itself. By quietly injecting malicious code into an upstream component that thousands of companies rely on, attackers gain an automatic backdoor into hundreds of corporate environments simultaneously. C. Identity as the New Attack Surface Attackers do not "hack" their way in using cinematic decryption tools; they simply log in using stolen credentials. Through phishing, credential stuffing, or purchasing stolen session tokens on the dark web, adversaries pose as legitimate users. If a network grants broad trust based purely on a correct password, the attacker inherits that trust instantly. 3. The Core Shift: Demystifying Zero-Trust The core philosophy of Zero-Trust is simple: Never trust, always verify. In a Zero-Trust architecture, the concept of a "trusted internal network" does not exist. Every request—whether coming from an unknown laptop in an airport cafe or an executive workstation inside headquarters—must prove its identity, validate its device health, and prove its authorization for every single interaction. Think of it like moving from a castle drawbridge to an international airport security model: Having an airline ticket does not let you wander onto the tarmac. You show your passport at the security line. You show your boarding pass at the gate. You are checked again as you step onto the aircraft. You are only permitted to sit in your designated seat, not enter the cockpit. How a Zero-Trust Policy Engine Evaluates a Request Every time an entity (a person or an automated software service) asks to read or write data, an automated "Policy Engine" inspects four distinct layers before granting access: Evaluation Factor What the System Checks Everyday Analogy Who is asking? Cryptographic identity, multi-factor authentication (MFA). Showing a government passport with a matching biometric scan. What device are they using? Device posture (operating system patched? disk encrypted? antivirus running?). Ensuring the vehicle entering a military base has passed safety inspections. Where are they located? Contextual clues (unusual time of day, anomalous geographic location, impossible travel speed). Flagging a credit card charge in Tokyo two hours after a purchase in London. What do they need? Least-privilege authorization (only the exact file or micro-service needed right now). A hotel keycard programmed to unlock only Room 304, and only until checkout. The Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP) Under Zero-Trust, access is no longer a blanket pass. It is granular and temporary. If an accountant needs to review a single invoice, they receive access only to that specific document for the duration of the task. They do not get read-access to the entire financial repository. 4. Architectural Resilience: Assuming the Breach Traditional security aimed for 100% prevention, an impossible standard in systems with millions of lines of code. Next-generation cybersecurity embraces an engineering reality known as Assume Breach. Resilience means accepting that software will have bugs, passwords will leak, and human users will occasionally click malicious links. The objective of the architecture is to guarantee that when a component fails or is compromised, the entire system does not collapse. A. Microsegmentation (Watertight Bulkheads) In maritime engineering, modern ships like ocean liners are divided into compartmentalized bulkheads. If a rock tears a hole in the outer hull, water fills only that single chamber. The water-tight doors slam shut, preventing the ocean from flooding the rest of the ship. In cybersecurity, this is called microsegmentation. Instead of a vast, flat corporate network where every device can talk to every other device, the digital ecosystem is divided into hundreds of isolated micro-zones: The web server can talk to the application server. The application server can talk to the database. The web server can never communicate directly with the database. Individual employee laptops cannot communicate with one another at all. If an attacker compromises one device, their "blast radius" is zeroed out. They are trapped inside that single isolated room. B. Security Chaos Engineering How do engineers know their defenses will hold during an attack? They deliberately simulate attacks during regular operations. Borrowed from Netflix's concept of the "Chaos Monkey," modern security teams use automated tools that deliberately shut down servers, revoke authentication certificates, or simulate rogue network traffic in real-time. By continuously exposing systems to artificial failures, the infrastructure develops an "immune system," learning to self-heal, reroute traffic, and isolate anomalies before a real adversary strikes. 5. The Evolution: Comparing Security Generations To see the complete picture, we can trace how cybersecurity has evolved across three major eras: Dimension Generation 1: Perimeter Defense Generation 2: Defense-in-Depth Generation 3: Zero-Trust & Resilience Primary Mindset Keep the bad actors out. Add layers (antivirus, email filters, firewalls). Assume breach; continuously verify everything. Network Structure Flat internal network; open communication inside. Segmented networks (VLANs, DMZ zones). Microsegmented; every service isolated by default. Trust Model Binary (Trusted inside / Untrusted outside). Role-based, long-lived access tokens. Context-driven, dynamic, least-privilege tokens. Defense Strategy Castle walls and static gatekeepers. Multiple checkpoints with delayed alerts. Automated immune response; self-healing workloads. 6. Emerging Frontiers: AI and the Post-Quantum Horizon As distributed ecosystems mature, two emerging forces are accelerating the need for architectural resilience: Artificial Intelligence at the Edge: Attackers now use machine-learning models to craft bespoke phishing emails in real-time and discover obscure configuration errors automatically. In response, modern defense systems rely on behavioral AI engines that spot anomalous activity in milliseconds—such as an internal account downloading files ten times faster than its daily average—and immediately sever its connection without waiting for human intervention. Post-Quantum Cryptography: The mathematical encryption algorithms safeguarding today's internet (such as RSA and ECC) will eventually be vulnerable to sufficiently powerful quantum computers. Resilient architecture requires "crypto-agility"—the capacity to swap out underlying encryption standards across distributed microservices via software updates, without needing to rewrite entire operating platforms. 7. Conclusion Next-generation cybersecurity is not a single product, firewall, or piece of software you can purchase and install. It is a fundamental philosophical and architectural shift. By abandoning the illusion of a secure perimeter and embracing the principles of Zero-Trust—continuous identity verification, ruthless application of least-privilege, and microsegmentation—modern systems ensure that a breach in one
